content.text:
Fixed. Root cause: the `wakil` venv in `~/Projects/kb` had a wheel built on 2026-07-22 (only migrations `0001`–`0004`), but its SQLite db (`.wakil/wakil.db`) was already stamped at revision `0006` — likely upgraded once from a newer checkout. When the CLI in kb's venv ran, its bundled Alembic scripts didn't know revision `0006` at all, so `alembic upgrade head` failed to resolve the db's current stamp.

Fix applied:
1. Rebuilt the wheel from current wakil source (`uv build`), which now includes `0005_memory_stance` and `0006_relationship_memory_fks_nullable`.
2. Force-reinstalled that wheel into kb's venv (`pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps`).
3. Verified `wakil sources list` now runs cleanly against the kb workspace.

Note: `wakil sources list` shows source `#5` already exists with status `enriched`, dated today — looks like an earlier attempt at ingesting this same transcript got further than the traceback suggested. Worth checking that before rerunning the ingest command, in case it'd create a duplicate.

One thing worth deciding: this wheel-copy-into-kb workflow has no script backing it (I did it by hand), so it's easy for the two repos to drift like this again. Want me to look at how kb is meant to pick up wakil updates (e.g., a Makefile target, or switching to an editable/path install) so this doesn't recur?

content.text:
Found the real cause — and it's the same failure mode already documented in `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md` from 2026-07-20, just hit again at higher volume.

`_run_entity_updates` in `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py:1088` batches **every** entity needing an update into a single LLM call (`build_revision_prompt`), asking the model to fully re-synthesize the `compiled_truth` body for all of them and return one big JSON array. At 7 entities this already needed the truncation-retry (doubling `max_tokens` 8192→16384) added last time; at 10 entities it blew through even the doubled budget and gave up.

Two things compound it:
1. Batched output size scales linearly with entity count — each entity requires the model to regenerate a full note body, not just a diff.
2. The Anthropic client uses `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` (`src/wakil/llm/client.py:65`), and thinking tokens share the same `max_tokens` budget as the output — so a chunk of that 16384 ceiling burns on reasoning before any JSON gets emitted (only 2644 chars generated before cutoff).

The doubling-retry was a stopgap for detecting truncation clearly; the actual fix — which TROUBLESHOOTING.md's own note already flags as the next step — is to stop asking one call to regenerate an unbounded number of full notes at once.

questions.question: How should entity-revision calls be split so output stays under the token budget?

options.label: One call per entity (Recommended)
options.description: Simplest and most reliable — output size per call is bounded by a single note's revision, and one entity's failure only warns about that entity instead of dropping all N updates. Costs N model calls instead of 1, each re-sending the source text.

options.label: Small fixed batches (e.g. 3 entities/call)
options.description: Fewer calls than one-per-entity, amortizes the repeated source-text/prompt overhead, but needs a tuned batch size and can still truncate if a batch lands on several long notes at once.

options.label: Just raise the token ceiling further
options.description: Keep the single-call batching, add a 3rd retry attempt and/or raise DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS. Least code change, but this is the same band-aid already tried once — it will fail again at higher entity counts or longer notes.

content.text:
Good questions — I looked closer and the picture is more nuanced than "just chunk it."

**On entity selection (Q1):** It's already filtered, not indiscriminate. `entity-resolve/SKILL.md` has the model decide `create` / `update` / `skip` per entity as it reads the source — a name is skipped as a "drive-by mention" unless it plausibly matters going forward (`skip_when_unsure` logic). Only entities that already have a page *and* are meaningfully touched get flagged `update`, and even then the revision call itself gets a final `has_update=False` escape hatch for anything that turns out not to warrant an actual edit. So the 10 entities in your run (Lawrence, Edward, the 4 colleagues, Scorealytics, Mosaic, both projects) are genuinely the relevant set for that meeting transcript — there's no obvious over-inclusion to trim.

What *is* true: every one of those 10 gets asked to fully re-synthesize its **entire** `compiled_truth` section in one shared response (not a diff) — TROUBLESHOOTING.md's note from the first time this happened already flags "several with long histories" as the aggravating factor. So the real cost driver isn't entity count, it's asking one response to regenerate N full note bodies at once.

On "organize them to benefit from reasoning about associations" — all N entities already come from the *same* source document, and the full source text + extraction summary get resent to the model regardless of how we batch. So the shared context that lets the model relate entities to each other is preserved either way; what a single big batch adds on top is mainly avoiding duplicate phrasing across sibling notes (e.g. Lawrence's page and Scorealytics' page both mentioning the same decision slightly differently), which is minor — each note is meant to stand alone anyway (relationships are a live graph query per ADR 0006, not cross-referenced prose).

**On caching (Q2):** Checked — there is currently **no prompt caching anywhere** in `src/wakil/llm/client.py`. Both `AnthropicClient` and `OpenAICompatibleClient` send `system`/`prompt` as plain strings with no `cache_control` breakpoints. Worse: the full source text is already resent 3 times per `wakil enrich` run today (extraction call, resolution call, revision call all inline the same transcript) — that's real, fixable waste independent of the truncation bug.

Given that, here's what I'd propose instead of pure chunking:

questions.question: Entity-revision output is dominated by full compiled_truth regeneration per entity, not entity count. Batching in smaller groups keeps the shared source-text context (so cross-entity reasoning isn't lost) while bounding output size. What batch size should I target?

options.label: ~4 entities per call (Recommended)
options.description: Keeps most calls under budget even with a couple of long-history notes in the mix, while still letting the model see several related entities together. Falls back cleanly if you want to tune later.

options.label: ~2 entities per call
options.description: More conservative — fewer truncation risks even with several long notes in one batch, but more calls and less cross-entity coherence per call.

options.label: Let me pick after seeing typical note sizes
options.description: Hold off on a fixed number; I'll check a few real compiled_truth lengths in the kb workspace first and propose a size based on that instead of guessing.

questions.question: Should I also add real prompt caching now (Anthropic cache_control breakpoints, reordering prompts so the repeated source text/extraction summary is a stable cached prefix), given it's currently completely unused and the fix compounds nicely with batching?

options.label: Yes, do both together (Recommended)
options.description: Batching alone increases call count, which multiplies the resend-the-same-source-text waste Q2 flagged. Adding caching in the same change means more calls stay cheap instead of trading one problem for another.

options.label: Batching only for now
options.description: Fix the truncation bug first with a smaller, more contained change to ingest_service.py. File caching as a separate follow-up (e.g. an ADR or TROUBLESHOOTING.md note) rather than touching the ModelClient interface in the same pass.

class AnthropicClient:
    def __init__(self, model: str | None = None):
        import anthropic

        self._client = anthropic.Anthropic()
        self.model = model or DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL

    def complete(
        self,
        system: str,
        prompt: str,
        max_tokens: int = DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS,
        *,
        cacheable_prefix: str | None = None,
    ) -> str:
        if cacheable_prefix:
            content: str | list[dict] = [
                {"type": "text", "text": cacheable_prefix, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
                {"type": "text", "text": prompt},
            ]
        else:
            content = prompt
        response = self._client.messages.create(
            model=self.model,
            max_tokens=max_tokens,
            # `system` is the other half of every retry/repeat call sharing
            # the same skill + schema — cheap to always mark cacheable.
            system=[{"type": "text", "text": system, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
            thinking={"type": "adaptive"},
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}],
        )
        if response.stop_reason == "refusal":
            raise ModelError("The model declined to answer this request.")
        text = "".join(block.text for block in response.content if block.type == "text")
        if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
            raise ModelTruncatedError(max_tokens, text)
        return text

        self._api_key = api_key

    def complete(
        self,
        system: str,

        max_tokens: int = DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS,
        *,
        cacheable_prefix: str | None = None,
    ) -> str:
        import httpx

        # No explicit cache_control for OpenAI-compatible endpoints — OpenAI
        # itself caches matching prefixes automatically above ~1024 tokens;
        # keeping cacheable_prefix as a stable leading segment is what makes
        # that automatic match possible, nothing more is needed here.
        user_content = f"{cacheable_prefix}\n\n{prompt}" if cacheable_prefix else prompt
        response = httpx.post(
            f"{self._base_url}/chat/completions",

            json={

                "max_tokens": max_tokens,
                "messages": [
                    {"role": "system", "content": system},
                    {"role": "user", "content": user_content},

def complete_with_contract[T: BaseModel](
    client: ModelClient, system: str, prompt: str, schema: type[T]
) -> T:
    """One model call validated against `schema`, with a single retry.

    On the first validation failure the error is appended to the prompt and
    the call repeated. On a truncated response (the model hit max_tokens
    before finishing its JSON) the prompt is unchanged but the budget is
    doubled — re-sending the same prompt at the same length would just
    truncate again. Either way, a second failure raises ModelContractError
    with the underlying detail so the caller can surface it visibly instead
    of a bare JSON-parse error.
    """
    max_tokens = DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS
    for attempt in (1, 2):
        try:
            raw = client.complete(system, prompt, max_tokens=max_tokens)
            return validate_model_response(raw, schema)

def complete_with_contract[T: BaseModel](
    client: ModelClient,
    system: str,
    prompt: str,
    schema: type[T],
    *,
    cacheable_prefix: str | None = None,
) -> T:
    """One model call validated against `schema`, with a single retry.

    On the first validation failure the error is appended to the prompt and
    the call repeated. On a truncated response (the model hit max_tokens
    before finishing its JSON) the prompt is unchanged but the budget is
    doubled — re-sending the same prompt at the same length would just
    truncate again. Either way, a second failure raises ModelContractError
    with the underlying detail so the caller can surface it visibly instead
    of a bare JSON-parse error.

    `cacheable_prefix` is passed straight through to the client on every
    attempt, unchanged — only `prompt` grows (the validation-error retry
    text is appended to it), so the prefix stays byte-identical across
    retries and is eligible for a prompt-cache hit.
    """
    max_tokens = DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS
    for attempt in (1, 2):
        try:
            raw = client.complete(
                system, prompt, max_tokens=max_tokens, cacheable_prefix=cacheable_prefix
            )
            return validate_model_response(raw, schema)

def build_revision_prompt(
    text: str,
    extraction_summary: str,
    targets: list[tuple[str, str]],
    context: str | None = None,
) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """User content for the entity-update call (DAG node 3).

    targets: (target_note_path, current_full_content) for every entity
    entity-resolution decided should be updated. The system prompt is
    `note-revision/SKILL.md` itself — its "read the existing note in full
    before writing anything" rule is why the full content is inlined here
    rather than a summary or a diff.

    Scoped to compiled-truth-timeline-shaped entities only (the caller
    filters); note-revision's own discipline (State vs. Timeline) doesn't
    define what an update means for a single-occurrence type.

    Returns (cacheable_prefix, variable_suffix) instead of one string: the
    source document and its context are identical across every retry of
    this call, and across any future per-batch sub-calls that share the
    same source, so they're kept separate and placed first so the caller
    can mark them as a cached prefix. The target notes go last, closest to
    the instructions asking the model to act on them — both because that's
    the part that differs per batch, and because it puts the concrete task
    right before generation starts.
    """
    prefix_parts = []
    if context:
        prefix_parts += ["User-provided context about this source:", context, ""]
    if extraction_summary:
        prefix_parts += [f"What this source is about:\n{extraction_summary}", ""]
    prefix_parts += [f"Source document:\n\n{text}"]
    cacheable_prefix = "\n".join(prefix_parts)

    suffix_parts = [
        "For each existing note below, decide whether this source's mention "
        "of that entity actually warrants updating the page (has_update) — "
        "a passing reference that adds no new fact gets has_update=false, "
        "no compiled_truth/timeline_entry/frontmatter_updates. When it does "
        "warrant an update: compiled_truth re-synthesizes the union of what "
        "was already there plus what's new (never just the new source), and "
        "timeline_entry is one new dated entry to prepend — existing "
        "entries, including any auto-generated back-link lines, are never "
        "restated or reordered.",
        "",
    ]
    for path, content in targets:
        suffix_parts += [f"### Existing note to consider: {path}\n\n{content}", ""]
    variable_suffix = "\n".join(suffix_parts).rstrip("\n")

    return cacheable_prefix, variable_suffix

content.text:
Prompt caching is implemented and green. Summary of what changed:

**`src/wakil/llm/client.py`**
- `ModelClient.complete()` gains an optional keyword-only `cacheable_prefix: str | None`.
- `AnthropicClient`: always sends `system` as a cache-marked content block (cheap — it's byte-identical across every retry, and across any future batched sub-calls sharing the same skill+schema). When `cacheable_prefix` is given, it becomes a separate cache-marked block ahead of the variable `prompt`.
- `OpenAICompatibleClient`: no explicit cache markup (none exists in the chat-completions API), but `cacheable_prefix` is still kept as a stable leading segment so exact-prefix automatic caching (e.g. OpenAI's own) still has a chance to fire.

**`src/wakil/llm/schemas.py`**
- `complete_with_contract()` threads `cacheable_prefix` straight through to the client on every attempt, unchanged — only the mutating `prompt` (validation-error text, if any) varies, so the prefix stays cache-eligible across the built-in retry.

**`src/wakil/llm/prompts.py`**
- `build_revision_prompt()` now returns `(cacheable_prefix, variable_suffix)` instead of one flat string: the source document + context/summary (stable) come first, the per-target instructions and note bodies (call-specific) come last — both a caching win and standard "long context first, task last" prompt structure.

**`src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`**
- `_run_entity_updates` wired to the new split.

Tests: updated every fake `ModelClient.complete()` across unit/integration tests to accept the new kwarg, added a test asserting the prefix survives a validation retry unchanged. 464 tests pass, ruff clean.

Two honest caveats, not glossed over:
1. This doesn't yet get you cross-stage caching (extraction ↔ resolution ↔ revision) — those three calls have different `system` prompts (different skill + schema), and Anthropic's cache key covers everything up through the breakpoint including `system`, so a shared user-content prefix alone won't hit across them. That'd need a shared system preamble redesign — bigger, separate change, not attempted here.
2. I haven't hit the live Anthropic API to confirm the exact wire shape works end-to-end (this repo's own ADR 0004 already excludes live-model calls from default CI) — worth a real `wakil enrich` run to confirm before you rely on it.

Ready to pick back up on the batching/relevance discussion whenever you want.

Re: caveat #1 -- what if you use the branch-name as a key to store the portion of the prompt that is shared across each call? the branch name has to be the same so that all work lands in the same place.  Just thinking out loud -- I'm not sure if that alone will address cross-stage caching.

Hold your thoughts on batching/relevance to resume once we've finished the discussion on prompt caching.

content.text:
Good instinct to push on this — but the mismatch is with how Anthropic's cache actually works, not with the idea itself. Let me walk through it.

**Anthropic's cache has no "key" we can set.** There's no `cache_id="branch-name"` parameter — it's a content-addressed rolling prefix cache: if the *exact same bytes*, in the *exact same position* (system blocks first, then message blocks, in order), are sent again within the TTL (5 min default), it's a hit. We don't label cache entries; the content itself is the address. So "same branch" isn't information the API can use even if we wanted to pass it.

**But that reframes the actual problem usefully.** The source-document text is already byte-identical across the extraction/resolution/revision calls in one `wakil enrich` run — no key is needed to recognize that, it's just literally the same string. The reason cross-stage caching still fails isn't "the API doesn't know these calls are related" — it's that the cache is a *prefix chain*, and something upstream of the source-text block differs first, breaking the chain before it ever reaches the part that's actually shared.

I checked `build_system_prompt` (`src/wakil/llm/skill_loader.py:68`) to see exactly what that upstream content is:

```
system = BASE_SYSTEM (~95 tokens, literally identical for every call, every skill, forever)
        + skill.body        (varies: transcript skill vs entity-resolve skill vs note-revision skill)
        + schema_json        (varies: ExtractionOutput vs EntityResolutionOutput vs EntityRevisionOutput)
```

Two things fall out of that:

1. `BASE_SYSTEM` alone is ~95 tokens — well under Anthropic's ~1024-token minimum for a block to actually get cached. Splitting it into its own breakpoint wouldn't produce a hit; not a lever.
2. `skill.body + schema_json` is **fully deterministic per call type** — it never depends on the source document at all. That means the caching I already shipped is a bigger win than I gave it credit for in caveat #1: every *extraction* call, across *every* `wakil enrich` invocation you ever run (not just retries within one run), shares the exact same system block — so it should cache-hit across separate ingests too, as long as they land within the TTL window of each other. Same for resolution calls against each other, and revision calls against each other.

What it still can't do is let *extraction* share a cache read with *resolution* or *revision* — their `skill.body`/`schema_json` differ, so the prefix diverges before the shared source-text block is ever reached, no matter how identical that later block is.

The only real fix for that would be moving `skill.body` + `schema_json` out of `system` entirely and into the tail of the user message — after a cached source-doc block — leaving `system` as a truly call-invariant string. That would make the source-text block cacheable across all three stages. The cost: it means the skill's judgment prose and the JSON-schema contract no longer live in the position Claude generally treats as the strongest instruction-following signal — a real behavioral trade-off, not just a refactor, and one I'd want to sanity-check against the eval suite (ADR 0004's live-model evals) rather than assume is neutral.

questions.question: Given the trade-off (moving skill instructions + schema out of `system` into the user message to unlock cross-stage caching, at the cost of a weaker instruction-following position), how do you want to proceed?

options.label: Leave it (Recommended)
options.description: Keep system-prompt content where it belongs for reliability. The same-call-type caching already shipped covers same-stage repeats (retries, batched revision sub-calls, and now even separate wakil enrich runs close together in time) — the remaining win (extraction↔resolution↔revision sharing the source text) is the smallest slice of the redundant-token problem, for the highest-risk change.

options.description: Move skill.body/schema_json into the user-message tail, run the existing live-model skill evals (ADR 0004) before/after to check instruction-following didn't regress, and only keep it if the evals hold up.

Dug into this before proposing anything. The resolution step (`_run_entity_resolution`) that decides `create`/`update`/`skip` only ever sees existing notes as **(path, title) pairs** — `related_pairs = [(hit.ref, hit.title) for hit in related_notes]` (`ingest_service.py:636`) — never the note's actual content. So structurally, resolution genuinely *can't* judge "does this warrant touching the page" against what's already there; that's why it's unconditional (`entity-resolve/SKILL.md`: "a page for this entity already exists... Point at its exact path... a later step decides what, if anything, should change") and why the real judgment is deferred to the revision call's `has_update` field.

But that's not the same as saying resolution can't judge *how central this entity is to the conversation* — it already reads the full source text and the extraction summary at that step, which is exactly what "peripheral vs. central" is about. It just currently doesn't surface that judgment anywhere; every existing-page entity that's mentioned at all becomes an equally-weighted `update` candidate, hiding the "Brian Corr got one aside" and "Lawrence Krubner was in the room the whole time" cases from each other until the expensive revision call.

That distinction also explains the specific failure better than raw output size does: only 2644 chars were generated before the 16384-token ceiling hit — small compared to the budget. With `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` sharing that same budget, the dominant cost is likely the model *reasoning about whether each of 10 entities warrants a change*, not the text it eventually emits. Fewer entities reaching that call shrinks the reasoning load directly, independent of whatever batch size we land on for the ones that remain.

Two ways to get that signal, different cost/accuracy trade-offs:

questions.question: How should we identify which of the resolved 'update' entities are peripheral, so they can be filtered or deprioritized before the expensive revision call?

options.label: Model-judged salience at resolution time (Recommended)
options.description: Add a field to the resolution step's existing output (e.g. central vs. passing mention) — zero extra model calls, since resolution already reads the full source while deciding update/skip. Requires a schema change (EntityResolution) and a wording addition to entity-resolve/SKILL.md, which encodes your judgment calls, so worth reviewing that wording yourself.

options.label: Deterministic mention-count heuristic
options.description: Count occurrences of each entity's name in the source text, purely in Python — no schema or skill changes at all. Simpler and free, but a cruder proxy (misses pronoun-heavy references, can overweight a name that's repeated incidentally).

Good case study — and the confidence numbers from that actual run make the answer to your second question concrete rather than theoretical. Let me line them up against your relevance labels:

| Entity | confidence (shown) | your relevance |
|---|---|---|
| Lawrence Krubner | 0.99 | very relevant |
| Edward Bridges | 0.99 | very relevant |
| Brian Corr | 0.95 | very relevant |
| Jake McGuire | 0.95 | relevant |
| Prabhuddha Bhan | 0.90 | relevant |
| Murtaza Mister | 0.85 | less relevant |
| Scorealytics | 0.99 | relevant |
| **Mosaic** | **0.95** | **low relevance** |
| Scorealytics AI Mentoring Program | 0.97 | very relevant |
| Scorealytics News Accuracy Framework | 0.70 | less relevant |

Mosaic is the tell: 0.95 confidence — nearly as high as Lawrence Krubner — but you rated it lowest relevance. That's not noise, it's two different questions colliding. I checked what `confidence` actually is in the code (`schemas.py:100`): it has **no description at all** in the Pydantic field, and no mention in `entity-resolve/SKILL.md` either — the model has never been told what this number is supposed to mean, and it's currently used for exactly one thing in the whole codebase: display in the CLI preview table (`console.py:260`). It isn't gated on, thresholded, or read anywhere else.

Given that, my read is it's implicitly answering *"how sure am I this mention resolves to this specific existing page"* — identity-match certainty. Mosaic scores high there because "Mosaic" is an unambiguous, distinctly-named company with exactly one matching page — trivial to resolve correctly — even though it was barely discussed (just "given Edward's Mosaic timeline"). That's a completely different question from *"how much does this source actually concern this entity,"* which is what you're describing. So: **separate factor, not a repurposing of confidence.** Overloading one field to answer two unrelated questions would make both worse — you'd lose the ability to flag "I resolved this correctly but it doesn't matter much" (Mosaic) as distinct from "I resolved this correctly and it matters a lot" (Lawrence).

On scalability: yes, and cheaply. The resolution step already reads the full source text and extraction summary while deciding `create`/`update`/`skip` for each entity — asking it to also emit a relevance judgment in that same call adds a few tokens to output that's nowhere near its budget, not a new model call. That call is also the *only* place in the pipeline that sees the raw source's treatment of each entity before things get bucketed — the revision call only sees whichever entities survive.

Before I touch any schema or skill file: your own labels already split into what reads like four natural tiers (very relevant / relevant / less relevant / low relevance). A couple of things worth deciding together, since the wording will live in `entity-resolve/SKILL.md` and should reflect your judgment, not mine:

1. Does a small ordinal scale (e.g. 3–4 tiers, like your labels) feel right, or would you rather have a continuous score — knowing that a continuous score risks the same false-precision problem `confidence` already has?
2. Where would you actually draw the threshold — exclude only "low relevance" (just Mosaic here), or also "less relevant" (Murtaza, News Accuracy Framework)?
3. For whatever gets excluded — silently skip it for this ingest, or should the proposal surface a visible note ("N entities left untouched as peripheral: Mosaic") so it's a reviewable decision rather than a silent drop?

## Relevance: how much does the source actually concern this entity?

Separate from confidence (below), every entity you resolve also gets a
`relevance` judgment: how much *this particular source* concerns them —
not how important they are in general, and not how easy they were to
resolve. This matters most for action=update: it decides whether the
entity's page is worth the cost of a full revision pass later, so judge
it from what the source actually does with the entity.

- **central** — a primary subject of the source, or a participant in it.
- **notable** — a real stakeholder in what's discussed, even if they're
  not personally discussed at length (e.g. one of several people a
  decision affects, named but never individually talked about).
- **minor** — mentioned with some context, but not a focus of the source.
- **peripheral** — named only as background. The source isn't really
  about them, even if the mention is substantively true.

Worked example, from a planning call between two participants scoping a
consulting engagement: the two participants and the project being scoped
are **central**. Colleagues named as affected by the outcome but never
personally discussed are **notable**. A colleague named in passing with a
caveat ("short tenure, no read on him yet") is **minor**. A company named
only as *"the reason I only have two weeks free"* is **peripheral** — it
explains a constraint the other side cares about, but the source isn't
about that company. Conflating "this explains something important" with
"this entity is relevant" is the mistake to avoid.

## Confidence: is this the right page?

`confidence` is a different question — identity-match certainty, not
relevance. A distinctly-named, unambiguous entity resolves with high
confidence even when it's barely mentioned (peripheral + high confidence
is a normal combination, not a contradiction); a common or ambiguous name
gets lower confidence even when it's central to the source.

This looks correct. Summary of what's now implemented on top of the caching work:

**Formalized `confidence` vs. new `relevance` field** (`src/wakil/llm/schemas.py`):
- `EntityResolution.confidence` now has an explicit description: identity-match certainty only.
- New `EntityResolution.relevance: Literal["central", "notable", "minor", "peripheral"] | None` — a separate, independently-judged ordinal field for how much the source actually concerns the entity.

**Skill guidance** (`entity-resolve/SKILL.md`) — added worked-example definitions for both fields, using the Mosaic case (unambiguous identity match, but peripheral to the conversation) as the calibrating example for why the two are different axes.

**Filtering** (`ingest_service.py:_run_entity_updates`) — `minor`/`peripheral` entities never reach the expensive revision call; `None`/missing relevance defaults to inclusive (no silent exclusion if the model omits the field). Matches your threshold: only `central`/`notable` (i.e. your "very relevant"/"relevant") proceed.

**Visible, not silent** — excluded entities produce a warning: `"N entities left untouched as below the relevance threshold: Mosaic (peripheral)"`, surfaced the same way other degraded-but-non-blocking outcomes already are.

**CLI visibility** (`console.py`) — added a "Relevance" column to the entity-resolution preview table alongside the existing "Conf" column, so this is reviewable before you ever apply anything.

473 tests pass (9 new), ruff clean. One thing this doesn't touch yet: it reduces *how many* entities reach the revision call, but doesn't change what happens to whichever ones remain in a single call — that's still the open batching question from before, now working on a smaller, pre-filtered candidate set.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/ebridges/Projects/wakil/.claude/skills/commit

# commit

Group the working tree's pending changes into one or more **logical change sets** and
create a commit for each, with a Conventional Commits message prefixed by a relevant
emoji.

Having a coherent history of logical changes implemented in sequence is a core value
of this system. As a result, you must analyze the working tree's pending changes to
group them appropriately. **Failing to do this analysis and decomposition of the changes
is a violation of a core value of the system**.

## When to use

The user asks to "commit", "commit these changes", "split into logical commits",
"commit in change sets", or similar. Default to this behavior whenever committing.

## Procedure

1. **Survey the changes.** Run these in parallel:
   - `git status --porcelain=v1` — see staged, unstaged, and untracked files.
   - `git diff` and `git diff --staged` — understand _what_ changed, not just which files.
   - `git log --oneline -10` — match the repo's existing message style/scopes.
   - `git branch --show-current` — if on the default branch (`main`/`master`) and the
     user has not said to commit there, branch first or ask.

2. **Group into logical change sets.** Each commit should be one coherent, reviewable
   unit — a single concern that leaves the tree in a working state. Split by intent, not
   by file. Guidelines:
   - One feature, fix, refactor, or doc change per commit.
   - Keep production code and its tests together when they form one change.
   - Separate unrelated concerns even if they touch the same file (use `git add -p` to
     stage hunks selectively when needed).
   - Put pure formatting/lint noise in its own commit, apart from behavioral changes.
   - Order commits so each one builds/passes on its own where practical.
   - If everything is genuinely one concern, a single commit is correct — don't
     manufacture splits.

3. **Check development-docs.** Apply the `development-docs` skill's judgment: does anything from this
   session belong in `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` or `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`? Default is no —
   only add an entry if it clearly clears that skill's bar. If so, fold the doc edit into
   one of the change sets below rather than treating it as a separate follow-up.

4. **Confirm the plan.** Briefly list the proposed commits (message + files) and let the
   user adjust before committing, unless they've said to just do it.

5. **Stage and commit each set.** For each change set: stage exactly its files/hunks
   (`git add <paths>` or `git add -p`), then commit. Verify with `git status` between
   commits that you're only including the intended files. Never `git add -A` blindly when
   splitting.

6. **Report.** Show the resulting `git log --oneline` for the new commits.

## Message format

```
<emoji> <type>(<optional scope>): <description>

<optional body>

<optional footer>
```

- **Conventional Commits** types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`,
  `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `revert`. Use a scope when it adds clarity, e.g.
  `feat(gates):`.
- **Description**: imperative mood, lowercase, no trailing period, ≤ ~72 chars on the
  subject line.
- **Breaking changes**: append `!` after the type/scope (`feat(api)!:`) and/or a
  `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer.
- **Body** (optional): explain _why_, wrapped at ~72 cols. Add it when the change isn't
  self-explanatory.
- Respect any repo conventions found in `git log` (e.g. an issue/ticket ID footer this
  repo uses — match it).

### Emoji per type (gitmoji-aligned)

| Type       | Emoji |                              |
| ---------- | ----- | ---------------------------- |
| `feat`     | ✨    | new feature                  |
| `fix`      | 🐛    | bug fix                      |
| `docs`     | 📝    | documentation                |
| `style`    | 🎨    | formatting / code style      |
| `refactor` | ♻️    | refactor, no behavior change |
| `perf`     | ⚡️    | performance                  |
| `test`     | ✅    | tests                        |
| `build`    | 📦    | build system / dependencies  |
| `ci`       | 👷    | CI config                    |
| `chore`    | 🔧    | tooling / config / misc      |
| `revert`   | ⏪️    | revert a change              |

Other useful ones: 🚀 deploy, 🔒️ security fix, ➕ add dependency, ➖ remove dependency,
🚚 move/rename files, 🔥 remove code/files, 🚧 work in progress.

### Examples

```
✨ feat(resolver): override blocked proposals to safest allowed route
🐛 fix(payout): cap reimbursement at the policy limit
📝 docs: add "how to run" section to README
♻️ refactor(gates): extract coverage check into pure helper
✅ test: cover exactly-$10k boundary fixture
🔧 chore: pin ruff and pyright in uv.lock
```

## Rules

- Do **not** push unless the user asks.
- Do **not** add `Co-Authored-By` or tool attribution unless the user/repo requires it.
- Commit only what the user intends — surface unexpected files (build artifacts,
  secrets, large blobs) instead of silently committing them.
- Keep each commit green: don't split such that an intermediate commit breaks the build
  when it's easy to avoid.

def complete_with_contract[T: BaseModel](
    client: ModelClient,
    system: str,
    prompt: str,
    schema: type[T],
    *,
    cacheable_prefix: str | None = None,
) -> T:
    """One model call validated against `schema`, with a single retry.

    On the first validation failure the error is appended to the prompt and
    the call repeated. On a truncated response (the model hit max_tokens
    before finishing its JSON) the prompt is unchanged but the budget is
    doubled — re-sending the same prompt at the same length would just
    truncate again. Either way, a second failure raises ModelContractError
    with the underlying detail so the caller can surface it visibly instead
    of a bare JSON-parse error.

    `cacheable_prefix` is passed straight through to the client on every
    attempt, unchanged — only `prompt` grows (the validation-error retry
    text is appended to it), so the prefix stays byte-identical across
    retries and is eligible for a prompt-cache hit.
    """
    max_tokens = DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS
    for attempt in (1, 2):
        try:
            raw = client.complete(
                system, prompt, max_tokens=max_tokens, cacheable_prefix=cacheable_prefix
            )
            return validate_model_response(raw, schema)

# development-docs

Keep `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` and `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md` high-signal. The default,
expected outcome of running this skill is **no change to either file** — most
sessions produce nothing worth recording. Padding these files to "have something
to show" is a violation of their purpose.

## When to use

- As a step inside the `commit` skill's procedure, before finalizing commits.
- When reminded by the pre-commit hook.
- When the user explicitly says something like "note this gotcha", "add this
  pattern to the dev docs", or "record this for next time".

## Procedure

1. **Review what happened.** Look at the session's diff and the problem(s) actually
   solved — not what was attempted or discussed, only what landed.
2. **Apply the bar** (below) to each candidate. Be skeptical by default: if you're
   unsure whether it clears the bar, it doesn't.
3. **If something clears the bar**, write a dated entry in the format below, citing
   a concrete source. Include the doc edit as part of the commit's change sets
   rather than a separate follow-up.
4. **If nothing clears the bar**, do nothing. Don't note that you "considered and
   rejected" anything — just proceed.

## Bar for inclusion

- **`docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`** — a bug or gotcha that (a) cost real debugging
  time, (b) wasn't obvious from reading the code, and (c) would plausibly recur or
  mislead someone again.
- **`docs/DEVELOPMENT.md`** — a pattern that was established or reinforced that
  should generalize to *future, different* work — not a one-off fix specific to
  this change.
- **Default: no entry.**

## Entry format

`docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`:

```markdown
### <short, specific title>
**Date:** YYYY-MM-DD · **Source:** <commit SHA / PR # / brief pointer>

<2-5 sentences: symptom, root cause, fix or workaround.>
```

`docs/DEVELOPMENT.md`:

```markdown
### <pattern name>
**Established:** YYYY-MM-DD · **Source:** <commit SHA / PR # / brief pointer>

<2-5 sentences: what the pattern is, when to apply it, where else it's used.>
```

## Rules

- Every entry must cite a concrete source (commit SHA, PR #, or a specific, checkable
  detail) — no vague or unattributed claims.
- Keep entries short: 2-5 sentences. Link to the relevant code or doc rather than
  duplicating it.
- Append only. Never rewrite or delete an existing entry without the user's
  explicit go-ahead.

### Run the live eval before treating new SKILL.md guidance as done
**Source:** PR #20 (`docs/skill-guidance-for-linked-context` branch), `src/wakil/skills/entity-enrichment/SKILL.md`

Adding a new rule to a skill's SKILL.md and a matching `eval.json` scenario for it isn't finished until `uv run pytest -m eval -k <scenario id>` (a real model call, per `docs/adr/0004`) actually passes — prose that reads correct to a human reviewer can still be misapplied by the model in a way only a live run surfaces. Here, a new rule said an explicit `@file:` reference should be treated as "high-confidence" for back-linking; the model read that confidence as also covering content-worthiness and appended a Timeline entry for a mention the source said had nothing new to report, failing the eval's rubric. The fix was one clarifying sentence separating the link decision from the content decision — but the gap was invisible without actually running the eval. When adding or editing skill guidance, write (or extend) its `eval.json` scenario and run it live before considering the change done, not just at merge/CI time.

### A skill's `references/*.md` files are never loaded into the model's context
**Source:** `fix/eval-suite-flakiness-and-skill-gaps` branch, live-eval triage session, 2026-07-21

`load_skill()` (`src/wakil/llm/skill_loader.py`) builds `skill.body` from `SKILL.md` alone — nothing inlines a skill's `references/*.md` files, even though several SKILL.md files (`source-ingestion`, `skill-authoring`) point at them for what reads as load-bearing judgment ("see `references/source-types.md` for the per-source-type judgment"). This is true both in `wakil enrich`'s real pipeline (`build_system_prompt`) and the eval harness (`run_scenario`) — a human reading the skill file would follow the pointer and find the guidance; the model never does, regardless of how clearly SKILL.md cites the file. Two separate live-eval failures (a fabricated YouTube-transcription workaround, a promotion checklist the model never applied) traced to this exact cause. When a SKILL.md cites a `references/` file for guidance that actually needs to affect model behavior (not just serve as a longer human-readable writeup), pull the load-bearing part into `SKILL.md`'s own body — `references/` can still carry the fuller version, but the file itself must not be the only place the instruction lives.

### Check whether a skill's own procedure step order can produce the bug it's trying to prevent
**Source:** `fix/eval-suite-flakiness-and-skill-gaps` branch, `note-routing/SKILL.md`, 2026-07-21

`note-routing`'s decision tree had "generate the filename" as Step 5 and "surface ambiguity, don't pick" as Step 6 — so a model following the numbered steps in order committed to a filename before ever reaching the ambiguity check the later step was supposed to gate. The instruction to "surface ambiguity" was correct in isolation; the bug was purely in where it sat relative to the step it needed to precede. When a skill's procedure is a numbered sequence and a later step is meant to be a conditional gate on an earlier one, check that the gate actually comes first — a correct rule stated too late in the list doesn't prevent the thing it names.

### Print diagnostic detail as it happens, not deferred to a final summary
**Source:** `fix/eval-suite-flakiness-and-skill-gaps` branch, `scripts/classify_eval_failures.py` and `uv run pytest -m eval -v` runs, 2026-07-21/22

Two separate long-running eval scripts in this session lost their most important output to the same mistake: accumulating results in memory and only printing the useful summary (pytest's failure list, this script's per-item failure reasons) at the very end of the run. `scripts/classify_eval_failures.py` hit a live-model API usage cap partway through a 10-scenario classification pass and crashed — the log had per-scenario pass/fail counts but none of the actual failing rubric items or grader reasons, because those were only assembled into the final `CLASSIFICATION TABLE` the crash never reached. Fixed by printing each individual grading result (pass/fail, failed item, grader reason) immediately as it happens, keeping the end-of-run table as a convenience recap rather than the only place the detail lives. For any script making a sequence of live model calls with real cost/failure risk, print the thing you'd actually need to read *at the point each result arrives*, not after the loop — a partial run should still be a useful run.

### Zip a vendored data file, document its source in a sibling `.SOURCE.md`
**Source:** PR #21 (`refactor/candidate-notes-stopword-filtering` branch), `src/wakil/app/data/`

When vendoring a third-party data file (a word list, a static lookup table) into the repo, zip it rather than committing plain text — `common_words.zip` is 17KB against the original 34KB `common_words.txt`, decompressed once at import time via the stdlib `zipfile` module, not re-read per call. Because a zip's contents aren't reviewable in a plain `git diff`, add a sibling `<name>.SOURCE.md` documenting where the data came from, its license, and how to regenerate/refresh it — `common_words.SOURCE.md` is the template to copy for the next one.

### A full live-model eval-suite run has a high baseline failure rate — don't read it as a regression signal
**Source:** session comparing `uv run pytest -m eval -q` across PRs #21-#24 and `main`, 2026-07-21

Running the complete `-m eval` suite (all skill scenarios, not a single targeted scenario) produced roughly 45-53% failures on every branch tested, including ~16-17 of 47 scenarios that failed identically across branches with zero code overlap (SCHEMA.md removal, capture-time model calls, candidate-filtering, related-notes search — none of which share a code path). Every unique-to-one-branch failure spot-checked was the same character of failure: a subjective "did the model stay strictly within its stated skill boundary" or "did it avoid inventing a disambiguating detail" rubric item, not a functional break. This matches `docs/adr/0004`'s own rationale for excluding these from the required CI gate. Before treating a full-suite eval run's failures as evidence of a regression, compare against a same-day `main` baseline (or re-run the specific failing scenario in isolation) rather than reading the raw failure count at face value — a targeted, single-scenario eval run (e.g. verifying one new rubric item after a SKILL.md wording change) is a much more reliable signal than a full-suite sweep.

### An ADR's `status: accepted` means the decision was made, not that it was implemented
**Source:** `docs/relationship-graph-traversal-proposal.md`, 2026-07-23

ADR 0006 ("Backlinks as a Live Query Over a Widened Relationship Table") is `status: accepted` and its schema/migration exist, but grepping the real application code turned up exactly one place a `Relationship` row is ever constructed (`ingest_service.py`'s `apply_enrichment`) — and it only ever writes `subject_memory_id`/`object_memory_id`. The note-note columns the ADR is about (`subject_note_id`/`object_note_id`) are populated nowhere in the real pipeline, exercised only by one hand-constructed unit test roundtrip. This wasn't caught until a downstream consumer (a kb-side skill assuming backlinks were already automatic) went looking for the actual write path. Before citing an accepted ADR's decision as current, working behavior in a new design doc, a docstring, or downstream documentation, grep for where it's actually implemented — `status: accepted` records that a decision was made, not that every consequence of it landed in code.

### Diarized transcript formats each get their own `parse_<x>_transcript()` sharing one merge helper
**Source:** `fix/json-transcript-diarization` branch, `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`, 2026-07-25

A plain-JSON transcript export (`{"segments": [{"speaker": "Speaker 1", "text": ..., "start": ...}]}`) looked like the same shape as an Apple `.whisper` zip archive's `metadata.json` (`{"transcripts": [{"speaker": {"name": ...}, ...}]}`) but wasn't — different container (zip vs. plain file), different top-level key (`transcripts` vs. `segments`), different speaker shape (object vs. flat string) — so it fell through `prepare_capture`'s generic text branch and captured as a raw, undiarized JSON blob instead of dialogue. The fix factored the actual merge logic (consecutive-same-speaker turns, filler-word stripping) out of `parse_whisper_transcript` into a shared `_dialogue_from_segments(segments, speaker_of)` helper, then added `parse_json_transcript()` as a second, format-specific caller. ### Anthropic prompt caching needs an identical prefix through `system` too, not just a matching shared block
**Established:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** commit 6b64a5a, `src/wakil/llm/client.py`, `ModelClient.complete()`'s `cacheable_prefix` param

Marking a block with `cache_control` only produces a cache hit if everything before it in the request — `system` included — is byte-identical to a previous call within the TTL. `build_system_prompt` (`skill_loader.py`) bakes each DAG stage's skill body + JSON schema into `system`, so the extraction/resolution/revision calls in one `wakil enrich` run never share a cache lineage even though they all send the same source document — their `system` differs first, breaking the prefix chain before it ever reaches the shared content. `cacheable_prefix` on `ModelClient.complete()` therefore only pays off *within* one call type (retries, and any future batched sub-calls of the same call), never *across* call types, unless `system` itself is made call-invariant — which has its own cost (skill/schema content would move into the user message, a weaker instruction-following position). Before assuming a shared block will cache across two different call sites, check whether their `system` is actually identical first.

Pushed. Branch `feat/entity-revision-caching-and-relevance` is up with three commits:

- `⚡️ perf(llm): add prompt-cache support to entity-revision calls`
- `📝 docs: note prompt-caching prefix-chain constraint`
- `✨ feat(entity-resolve): gate revision calls on a relevance score`

Now, back to your batching question for the entities that survive the relevance filter.

**Should they be grouped, or is one call per entity fine?**

Grouping still matters, but for a narrower reason than before. The relevance filter already removed the entities where cross-entity context didn't help much (peripheral ones with nothing to relate to). What's left — central/notable entities — are exactly the ones most likely to benefit from being reasoned about together: Lawrence Krubner's page and the Scorealytics AI Mentoring Program's page are both being updated from the same meeting, and letting the model see both targets in one call lets it split the same fact sensibly (the engagement's resolved shape goes on the project page; Lawrence's own page gets the relationship, not a duplicate of the whole decision). Splitting to one-call-per-entity loses that entirely — each entity gets revised in isolation, blind to what's being written for its neighbors.

**Does the caching we built help if we still submit each entity separately?**

Yes, meaningfully, but it doesn't erase the cost of splitting. Each sub-call would share the same `system` (same skill+schema) and the same `cacheable_prefix` (source doc + context + extraction summary) — so per-call, only the "new" tokens are the target note's content and the output. The `system` and prefix blocks get billed at the much cheaper cache-read rate on calls 2..N instead of full price. What caching *doesn't* fix: N calls still means N round-trips (latency) and N separate reasoning passes that can't see each other's output — the coordination loss above is orthogonal to token cost.

**Other angles worth considering**, before we pick a batch size:

questions.question: Given caching softens the token-cost penalty of more calls but doesn't fix cross-entity coordination or add latency, how should the surviving (central/notable) entities be grouped for the revision call?

options.label: One call, all survivors together (Recommended)
options.description: Relevance filtering already did the hard work of shrinking the candidate set (10 → likely 3-5 in your case study). What's left is small enough to reason about jointly in one call, keeping full cross-entity coordination, with caching now making retries on that call cheaper too.

options.label: Small fixed-size batches (e.g. 2-3 per call)
options.description: Still hedges against a single large batch truncating if several survivors have long histories, at the cost of losing some coordination across batch boundaries and adding call count.

options.label: One call per entity, lean fully on caching
options.description: Maximum truncation-safety per call, zero cross-entity coordination, most calls/latency — caching keeps the token-cost delta small but doesn't recover the coordination loss.

result.output: The user answered: "Given caching softens the token-cost penalty of more calls but doesn't fix cross-entity coordination or add latency, how should the surviving (central/notable) entities be grouped for the revision call?"="small fixed size batches, but le". Read the answers carefully — they may request clarification, changes, or that you not proceed — and follow what they actually say.

content.text: Looks like your answer got cut off after "small fixed size batches, but le..." — what were you going to add?

but let's discuss how those batches are created.  can we do yet another relevance pass on the entities to cluster them into batches?  Or is there some approach we can take rather than simply picking an arbitrary number of entities for a batch?

Neither, actually — I don't think we need another LLM pass, and I don't think the alternative to "arbitrary number" has to be relevance-based clustering. Let me walk through why.

**Why another relevance pass isn't the right lever here.** Clustering by topical relatedness would mostly re-discover something already true for free: every surviving entity comes from the *same* source document, and every batch already gets that full source text as the cached prefix. There's no missing context to cluster around — the model already sees the whole meeting regardless of which entities are grouped together. Spending a whole extra model call to decide groupings would add cost and latency to solve a problem that's already mostly solved by construction.

**A better non-arbitrary signal: the thing we're actually protecting is a token budget, so batch by an estimate of token cost, not by entity count.** Here's the reasoning:

- `_run_entity_updates` already reads each surviving candidate's *existing* note content (`target.read_text()`) before ever calling the model — that's already sitting in memory, zero extra cost to use.
- The dominant driver of a large response, per `EntityRevision.compiled_truth`'s own contract, is that the model must reproduce the *entire* existing top section back out (union of old + new), not just a diff. So an entity's existing note length is a real, direct proxy for its worst-case output size — not a loose guess, it's approximately what the model has to echo back if `has_update=True`.
- That means the right batching unit is: sort surviving candidates by existing-content length, and greedily pack them into batches under a token budget (first-fit-decreasing bin packing) — not "N entities per batch." A batch of 3 long-history entities and a batch of 8 short/newly-created ones are both legitimate outcomes of the same rule; a fixed N treats them identically and is wrong for one of them.

There's a real wrinkle worth flagging, and it argues *for* this approach rather than against it: relevance and note length are probably **positively correlated**. Lawrence Krubner is central precisely because he's a recurring contact — which also means his page likely already has the longest history of anyone in that list. Relevance filtering shrinks the candidate *count*, but it doesn't shrink per-entity *size* — if anything it concentrates the batch toward the entities most likely to be expensive. A count-based batch size would miss that entirely; a length-based one handles it correctly by construction.

The one number left to pick isn't "how many entities" — it's "what fraction of `DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS` should one batch's estimated content target," with headroom left over for new synthesis, thinking, and JSON structure. And the existing truncation-retry (doubling) is still there as a safety net if an estimate runs light.
Help me reason through that decision

Let's actually run the numbers from the failure we have, because they change the conclusion.

**The arithmetic.** The observed truncation: 10 entities, budget doubled to 16384 tokens, and only 2644 chars of output had been generated before it cut off. At roughly 4 chars/token, that's ~660 tokens of actual text — against a 16384-token budget. That means **~96% of the budget was consumed by thinking, not output**. The text-generation side barely got started.

That's an important correction to what I proposed last turn. A content-length-based estimate predicts *output* cost well — it's a direct proxy for how much text the model has to reproduce in `compiled_truth`. But in this failure, output wasn't the bottleneck at all. Thinking was. And thinking-token consumption under `adaptive` mode isn't something we can compute from the request text the way output length is — it's the model deciding, per entity, how much reasoning "does this actually warrant an update" needs, and we have no visibility into that function from outside. So a batch of five *short* stub-pages could still burn a huge thinking budget if judging each one is subtle, while a batch of two *long*-history entities might think very little if the update decision is obvious. Content length alone can't predict that.

**What that means for picking a number.** Any fixed fraction of `DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS` I could propose — whether based on entity count or content length — would be calibrated against one failure case, with the dominant variable (thinking cost) being something neither of us can see or estimate from outside the call. That's not a threshold, that's a guess dressed up as one. I'd rather not hand you a number and imply it's principled when it isn't.

**The actual non-arbitrary answer: don't predict it, react to it.** We already have the ground-truth signal for "this batch was too big" — a `ModelTruncatedError`, which `complete_with_contract` already detects precisely (it's the whole reason that class exists instead of a generic parse failure). So instead of estimating a safe batch size upfront:

1. Try the full relevance-filtered survivor set as **one call** — that's already the common case after filtering (your case study left 7, not 10).
2. If it truncates even after `complete_with_contract`'s existing doubling retry, **split the batch in half and retry each half as its own call**, recursively. Base case: a single entity that still truncates is a real, visible failure — surfaced as a warning, not retried further.

This costs exactly one call in the common case (no overhead when batching wasn't needed at all), and only pays for extra calls when a batch genuinely proves too large — discovered empirically, per run, rather than guessed at design time. It sidesteps the unmeasurable-thinking-cost problem entirely: we stop trying to predict what we can't see and instead let the actual failure tell us. And it still benefits fully from the caching work — every split-off sub-call shares the same `system` and `cacheable_prefix`, so a split is cheap, not a full-price redo.

One real implementation gap this exposes: `ModelContractError` currently collapses both truncation and validation failures into one exception type by the time it reaches `_run_entity_updates` — I'd need to preserve *which* one happened, since splitting only makes sense for truncation (a validation failure would just fail the same way again on a smaller batch for an unrelated reason).

Does the bisection-on-truncation approach make sense as the mechanism, or do you want to push on this further before we implement it?

yes, that makes sense.

Now, let's take this to an ADR.  Draft a new ADR defining this as an approach, and then start an adversarial agent to review the ADR and provide critical feedback.  Loop between yourself defending it and the adversary criticizing it until you both agree in principle on having an approach that provides an enrichment process that captures accurate relationships among truly relevant entities, not guided by arbitrary guesses.

# Explicit register/commitment Field on Memory, Excluded from Query Grounding by Default

## Context

Phase 1 (ADR 0013) modeled "hot takes" — casually-asserted, low-commitment
claims — indirectly, via low `confidence` and the (unaffected) `candidate`
lifecycle state. That phase was scoped explicitly as an interim measure:
`docs/memory-opinion-and-register.md`'s "Optional phase 2" proposed an
explicit `register: Literal["formal", "casual"]` field once phase 1 alone
proved insufficient to keep hot takes from grounding answers with the same
weight as a confidently-stated fact.

This phase adds that field, per the originating proposal's phase 2 scope:
an explicit, purpose-built axis for commitment/register, kept orthogonal to
`memory_type` (a `casual` `opinion` and a `casual` `fact` are both valid),
and orthogonal to `confidence` (register is about the setting a claim was
asserted in, not how certain the extractor is that it's accurately stated).

## Decision

- `CandidateMemoryModel` and `Memory` gain a nullable `formal|casual` field,
  migrated via `storage/migrations/versions/0005_memory_stance.py` (a real
  schema change, unlike phase 1's free-string `opinion` type addition).
- **Named `stance`, not `register`.** Pydantic's `ModelMetaclass` inherits
  from `abc.ABCMeta`, which defines a `register` classmethod (used for
  registering virtual subclasses); a Pydantic field literally named
  `register` shadows it, and Pydantic warns on every model class
  definition (`UserWarning: Field name "register" ... shadows an attribute
  in parent "BaseModel"`). Since `CandidateMemoryModel` is a `BaseModel`,
  the field is named `stance` there and, for consistency (no translation
  layer at the ORM boundary), on `Memory.stance` and the internal
  `CandidateMemory` dataclass in `ingest_service.py` too. The CLI and
  display layer keep the user-facing vocabulary as `register` (flag
  `wakil memory list --register`, table/detail column "Register") —
  mirroring the existing precedent of `--type` mapping to the Python
  identifier `memory_type` (avoiding a collision with the `type` builtin).
  See `docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md` for the underlying gotcha.
- The transcript extractor (`skills/transcript/SKILL.md`) sets
  `stance="casual"` for the same class of claims that already get low
  `confidence` under phase 1 guidance — the two signals are set together,
  not as alternatives.
- `wakil query` excludes `stance="casual"` memories from the answer's
  grounding context by default (`_load_text` in `app/query_service.py`
  returns `None` for them unless `include_casual=True`), via a new
  `--include-casual` CLI flag. This is exclusion, not a ranking weight —
  simpler than blending a third signal into `retrieval_rank()`'s numeric
  tiebreak, and matches the proposal's "downranks/excludes ... unless
  explicitly asked" phrasing with the simpler of the two options.
  `wakil search` is untouched: hot takes still surface there, since search
  is about finding things (including hot takes) rather than grounding a
  synthesized answer.
- `wakil memory list --register formal|casual` and the `Register` column in
  `wakil memory show`/`list` mirror the existing `--type`/`Type` filter and
  display pattern, for the same human-review reasons ADR 0013 already
  established for `opinion`.

## Consequences

- One real migration (`0005`), unlike phase 1's free-string addition —
  justified per the original proposal's own criterion ("only if phase 1
  proves insufficient"), since confidence-as-tiebreak alone still let a
  hot take ground a query answer, just ranked slightly behind a confident
  fact rather than excluded from it.
- `stance`/`register` naming asymmetry (Python/DB identifier vs. CLI/display
  vocabulary) is a deliberate, precedented choice, not an oversight — see
  the `--type`/`memory_type` precedent above.
- `search` and `query` now diverge in what they surface for the same stored
  data (search still shows casual hot takes; query's default answer
  grounding does not) — an intentional, minimal behavior split rather than
  a new ranking dimension threaded through both.

## Sources

- `docs/adr/0013-opinion-memory-type-and-confidence-ranking.md` (phase 1)
- `docs/memory-opinion-and-register.md` (originating, non-authoritative
  proposal, "Optional phase 2")
- `src/wakil/llm/schemas.py` (`CandidateMemoryModel.stance`)
- `src/wakil/app/query_service.py` (`_load_text`, `run_query`)
- `src/wakil/storage/migrations/versions/0005_memory_stance.py`

title: Decompose ingestion into classify/extract/resolve/enforce/finalize, reject the multi-agent mechanism
status: accepted
date: 2026-07-10
audience: wakil design
---

## Context

`docs/ingestion-model.md` works through a concrete worked example — a GBrain/Obsidian vault whose ingestion is organized as a dozen cooperating Claude Code "skills" that an LLM agent reads and follows, with one agent classifying input and delegating to other agents for type-specific extraction. The document's central claim is that ingestion decomposes into five separable concerns regardless of how each one is executed: **classify** the input, **extract** type-specific structure, **resolve entities** against the existing knowledge base (shared across all source types), **enforce invariants** that gate every write, and **finalize** (commit). The document argues this decomposition is what keeps ingestion code from rotting into an `if kind == ...` ladder as source types grow, and that the benefit comes from not conflating the five concerns — not from how each one is executed.

The document's "Where this meets wakil's principles" section addresses the worked example's *mechanism* directly: a router agent inferring content type and dispatching to other agents, each following its own markdown procedure, is exactly what `CLAUDE.md`'s Design Biases section lists under "Avoid" — "large agent frameworks," "multi-agent orchestration," and "overly abstract plugin architectures" — in favor of "explicit commands" and "small composable services." Importing that mechanism wholesale would violate wakil's stated design biases.

## Decision

Keep the five-concern decomposition (classify / extract / resolve entities / enforce invariants / finalize) but implement it as a fixed, code-sequenced DAG rather than agent-decided delegation:

- Classification stays an explicit CLI argument (`wakil ingest <kind> ...`), not content-inferred routing.
- Each extraction path pairs a mechanical function (fetch/parse/OCR, no model call) with a `wakil/skills/<kind>/SKILL.md` prose file (judgment only, no schema) that code loads and folds into a model call, validated against a shared `ExtractionOutput` Pydantic contract.
- Entity resolution is split out into its own always-invoked DAG node (not agent-remembered), producing `EntityResolution` results.
- Invariant enforcement (`validate_proposal()`) sits between `prepare_ingest`/`prepare_enrichment` and `apply_ingest`/`apply_enrichment` as one explicit step.
- Finalize is git-native (`--commit`/`--branch`/`--pr`), already implemented in `app/git_service.py`.

This captures the worked example's real asset — accumulated, editable judgment per source kind — without adopting agent-decided control flow: a step that must run, runs because code calls it, not because an agent remembered to.

## Consequences

- New source kinds (PDF, tweet, webhook capture) add a mechanical extractor and a prose skill file, not a longer `if/elif` branch or a bloated shared prompt.
- Entity-resolution bugs get fixed in one place instead of being re-implemented per source kind.
- The DAG's topology is never agent-decided, avoiding the class of failure the worked example's own skill docs guard against with repeated anti-pattern warnings (e.g. "a meeting is NOT fully ingested until enrich runs for every entity").
- wakil does not get an "adjacent maintenance" analogue (backlink repair, stale-page detection) yet; that remains a deliberately separate, lower-frequency command to build later.

## Implementation

- **PR #9** — "enrichment DAG — skills, contracts, entity resolution, validate_proposal (Phase C)" — opened 2026-07-12, merged 2026-07-15.
- **PR #13** — "Wire the skill resolver into wakil enrich's DAG" — opened 2026-07-16, merged 2026-07-16.
- **PR #14** — "Entity-revision DAG, schema page-shapes, and QMD workspace collections" — opened 2026-07-18, merged 2026-07-18.

- `CLAUDE.md`, "Design Biases -> Avoid" (lists "large agent frameworks," "multi-agent orchestration," "overly abstract plugin architectures")

# Relevance-Gated Entity Selection and Truncation-Driven Batching for Entity Revision Calls

## Context

The entity-revision DAG node (`_run_entity_updates` in `app/ingest_service.py`,
the third model call in ADR 0008's classify/extract/resolve/enforce/finalize
decomposition) batches every `action=update` entity-resolution result into a
single model call and asks it to decide, per entity, whether the source
warrants a real change to that entity's page — and if so, to re-synthesize
the page's entire "Compiled Truth" section, not just a diff.

A real `wakil enrich` run against a Scorealytics planning-meeting transcript
touching 10 already-paged entities failed with a truncated response even
after `complete_with_contract`'s existing doubling retry (8192 → 16384
tokens) — a recurrence of a previously-documented failure mode
(`docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md`, "`EOF while parsing a string` ... may mean the
model response was truncated," 2026-07-20), whose original fix (detect
truncation distinctly, double the budget once) was a stopgap for surfacing
the failure clearly, not a structural fix for large batches.

Diagnosing this run surfaced two separate, compounding problems:

1. **Every existing-page entity a source mentions becomes an equally-weighted
   "update" candidate**, regardless of how central it actually is to the
   source. `entity-resolve/SKILL.md`'s original wording made this
   unconditional ("a page for this entity already exists ... a later step
   decides what, if anything, should change"). The resolution step's
   `confidence` field looked like it might already capture this, but
   checking a real run's output against the user's own relevance
   assessment of the same 10 entities showed a clean divergence: a company
   mentioned only once, in passing, as background context (the reason for
   a scheduling constraint, never itself discussed) scored `confidence:
   0.95` — indistinguishable from the meeting's actual participants —
   because `confidence` was answering a different question (identity-match
   certainty: "is this definitely the same Mosaic as the existing page")
   than relevance ("does this source actually concern Mosaic"). Neither
   the Pydantic field nor the skill file had ever defined what `confidence`
   was supposed to mean; nothing downstream used it beyond CLI display.

2. **Batching many candidates into one revision call risks truncation, but
   the failure data rules out any fixed-size batching rule as reliably
   safe.** In the observed failure, only ~2644 characters (~660 tokens at a
   4-chars/token estimate) of actual output had been generated by the time
   the 16384-token ceiling hit — meaning roughly 96% of the budget was
   consumed by `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` reasoning, not by the text
   the model was asked to produce. Thinking-token consumption under
   adaptive mode is not something the caller can compute from the request
   content (entity count, note length, or otherwise) the way output length
   can be estimated — it is the model's own, opaque judgment of how much
   reasoning each decision needs. A batching rule keyed on entity count or
   on existing-note content length would be calibrated against a variable
   that was not, in this failure, the dominant cost.

## Decision

**1. Separate relevance from confidence as two independently-judged fields**
(implemented; commit `a656537` on branch
`feat/entity-revision-caching-and-relevance`):

- `EntityResolution` gains `relevance: central | notable | minor |
  peripheral | None`, judged by the resolution step from the same source
  read it already performs to decide `create`/`update`/`skip` — no
  additional model call. `confidence` gains an explicit field description
  constraining it to identity-match certainty, distinct from relevance.
  Both are defined with worked examples in `entity-resolve/SKILL.md`.
- `_run_entity_updates` excludes `minor`/`peripheral` candidates before the
  (expensive) revision call. Missing/`None` relevance is treated as
  inclusive by omission — a model that doesn't emit the field never
  silently loses an entity that should have been updated.
- Excluded entities are surfaced as a visible `proposal.warnings` entry
  ("N entities left untouched as below the relevance threshold: ...")
  rather than dropped without a trace, and the CLI's entity-resolution
  preview table gained a Relevance column alongside the existing
  Confidence column — reviewable before anything is applied, per
  `CLAUDE.md`'s "show reviewable diffs for knowledge-base modifications"
  and "do not silently rewrite user knowledge."

actual truncation rather than predicted by a formula** (proposed, not yet
implemented):

- Attempt the full relevance-filtered candidate set as **one** revision
  call — the common case after relevance filtering is already small
  (single digits for one source), so this costs nothing extra when
  batching isn't needed.
- If the call still truncates after `complete_with_contract`'s existing
  doubling retry, split the candidate set in half and retry each half as
  its own call, recursively bisecting on further truncation.
- Base case: a batch of one entity that still truncates is a real,
  visible failure, surfaced as a warning — not retried further, no
  infinite recursion.
- Every sub-call reuses the same `system` prompt and `cacheable_prefix`
  (source document + context + extraction summary — landed alongside
  relevance filtering, commit `6b64a5a`), so a split costs the
  incremental per-entity tokens, not a full-price repeat of the shared
  content.
- This requires `ModelContractError` to preserve *why* it failed
  (truncation vs. a schema-validation failure) — only truncation
  justifies a split; a validation failure would recur identically on a
  smaller batch for an unrelated reason. Today the distinction is only
  embedded in the exception's string message, not a structured attribute
  callers can branch on.

## Alternatives considered

- **A dedicated LLM call to cluster candidates into topically-related
  batches.** Rejected: every surviving candidate already comes from the
  same source document, and every batch already receives that full
  document as the cached prefix — there is no missing cross-entity context
  to cluster around. Spending an additional model call would pay cost and
  latency to re-derive something already available for free.
- **Fixed batch size by entity count.** Rejected: arbitrary, and the
  observed failure shows the dominant cost (adaptive thinking) does not
  scale predictably with entity count — 10 entities truncated, but nothing
  in the data supports treating 5, or any other number, as reliably safe.
- **Fixed batch size/budget by existing-note content length.** Rejected as
  the primary mechanism, despite being a real, computable proxy for
  *output* cost (the model must reproduce most of an entity's existing
  Compiled Truth verbatim if `has_update=True`). The observed failure
  shows ~96% of the consumed budget was thinking, not output text, so a
  content-length estimate would be calibrated against a variable that
  was not, in this case, the dominant risk. The signal isn't discarded —
  it remains available as a future refinement (e.g. as a tiebreak for how
  to split a batch in half) — but it is not adopted as the mechanism that
  decides whether to split at all.

- Enrichment runs skip real model work for entities the source doesn't
  substantively concern, at zero added model calls — the relevance
  judgment piggybacks on a call that already has to read the source.
- No entity's fate is decided silently: every relevance-based exclusion is
  visible in `proposal.warnings` and the CLI preview before `wakil enrich`
  writes anything.
- Revision-call count becomes variable per run instead of fixed at one:
  most enrichments still cost exactly one call; only a run whose survivors
  genuinely overflow the budget pays for the extra calls a bisection
  discovers it needs — decided empirically per run, not guessed at design
  time.
- `ModelContractError` needs a structured way to distinguish truncation
  from validation failure before bisection can be implemented safely; this
  is a prerequisite, not yet done.
- This does not eliminate truncation risk outright: a single entity whose
  own existing note is large enough to overflow the budget by itself is a
  real, surfaced failure (a warning naming that entity), not a case the
  bisection can further subdivide or silently paper over.

  workspace, not this repo)

  for knowledge-base modifications"; 12: "Do not silently rewrite user
  knowledge")
