+### Anthropic prompt caching needs an identical prefix through `system` too, not just a matching shared block
+**Established:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** commit 6b64a5a, `src/wakil/llm/client.py`, `ModelClient.complete()`'s `cacheable_prefix` param
+
+Marking a block with `cache_control` only produces a cache hit if everything before it in the request — `system` included — is byte-identical to a previous call within the TTL. `build_system_prompt` (`skill_loader.py`) bakes each DAG stage's skill body + JSON schema into `system`, so the extraction/resolution/revision calls in one `wakil enrich` run never share a cache lineage even though they all send the same source document — their `system` differs first, breaking the prefix chain before it ever reaches the shared content. `cacheable_prefix` on `ModelClient.complete()` therefore only pays off *within* one call type (retries, and any future batched sub-calls of the same call), never *across* call types, unless `system` itself is made call-invariant — which has its own cost (skill/schema content would move into the user message, a weaker instruction-following position). Before assuming a shared block will cache across two different call sites, check whether their `system` is actually identical first.
+
+### `thinking.budget_tokens` doesn't exist on `claude-opus-4-8` and later — use `output_config.effort` or `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` instead
+**Established:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** `docs/adr/0015-relevance-gated-entities-and-truncation-driven-batching.md` (Decision 2, Step A), `src/wakil/llm/client.py`'s `DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL`
+
+`AnthropicClient.complete` hardcodes `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` with no way to bound how much of `max_tokens` thinking consumes before output starts. The obvious lever — `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` — returns a 400 error on `claude-opus-4-8` (this codebase's `DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL`) and every later model in the family (Opus 4.7+, Fable 5, Mythos 5), confirmed against Anthropic's live migration guide (platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/migration-guide.md) and not just assumed. The two levers that are actually available on this model, confirmed against the installed SDK's type stubs (`anthropic` package, `types/output_config_param.py`, `types/thinking_config_disabled_param.py`): `output_config={"effort": "low"|"medium"|"high"|"xhigh"|"max"}` (compatible with adaptive thinking, currently never set — the call runs at whatever server-side default applies), and `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` (eliminates thinking-token cost entirely, at the cost of whatever quality adaptive thinking buys). Before adding a `budget_tokens` cap to any Anthropic call in this codebase, check the current model's actual capability — model-specific thinking/effort support changes across the Claude model lineage, and a docs page is one step removed from observed behavior, so verify with a live call before relying on either lever in production.

## Summary

Fixes a real production `wakil enrich` truncation failure (`ModelContractError` on the entity-revision call), via ADR 0015. Three changesets:

- **Prompt caching** — `system` and a `cacheable_prefix` (source doc + context) are marked for Anthropic prompt caching, cutting cost on retries and future batched sub-calls.
- **Relevance-gated entity selection** — `EntityResolution` gains a `relevance: central|notable|minor|peripheral` field, judged for free during entity resolution (no extra model call). `_run_entity_updates` excludes `minor`/`peripheral` candidates before the expensive revision call, surfaced as a visible warning rather than a silent drop. `confidence` gets an explicit description clarifying it's identity-match certainty, not relevance — these were previously conflated.
- **Truncation-driven bisection** — `ModelContractError` now carries a `truncated: bool` so callers can distinguish "hit the token budget" from "produced malformed JSON." On a truncated revision call, `_revise_candidates` splits the batch by existing-note content length (isolating the largest note first) and retries each half recursively, capped at `_MAX_BISECTION_DEPTH = 3` to bound worst-case fan-out.

All three decisions are backed by live experiments against the real Anthropic API and the actual originally-failing transcript — not just design reasoning. See `docs/adr/0015-relevance-gated-entities-and-truncation-driven-batching.md` for the full case study, the rejected alternatives (including a live-tested "bound the thinking budget directly" approach that turned out not to work), and the adversarial review this ADR went through before being accepted.

## Test plan

- [x] `uv run ruff check` — clean

- [ ] Live-model eval for the new `relevance` judgment (ADR 0015 names this as a required follow-up, not yet done — tracked in the ADR itself)
EOF

**Date:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** PR #32 (`feat/entity-revision-caching-and-relevance`), adversarial PR review

ADR 0015's Decision 2 (Step B: bisect a truncating entity-revision batch) was implemented, unit-tested (479 passed), and live-validated against the real originally-failing transcript — but the working tree was never `git commit`ed before a `wakil enrich` live-validation run and, separately, a PR was opened (`gh pr create`) claiming the change as shipped. In between, the shared working directory got checked out to `main` for an unrelated commit (another actor, same checkout) — something in that sequence stashed the uncommitted Step B changes (`git stash list` showed `wip: entity-revision-caching-and-relevance (untouched by ADR 0016 commit)`, so the stash itself was made carefully, but nothing surfaced it as still-pending work afterward). The PR was opened against the branch's last *committed* state — one commit behind — so the PR's description described real, tested code that was not actually present in the diff. An adversarial PR-review pass caught the discrepancy immediately by grepping the diff for the claimed function names and finding nothing.

Nothing was lost — `git stash list` still had it, `git stash pop` recovered it cleanly, and re-running the test suite confirmed it matched what had been validated. But the near-miss is the lesson: **run `git status` and `git diff <base>...<branch>` immediately before `gh pr create`, not from memory of having committed** — a shared working tree can be modified by activity outside the current tool-call history (another session, another terminal, the user's own git commands) between when work is done and when a PR is opened, and neither `pytest` passing nor a live validation run having happened proves the code that was tested is the code that's committed.

49	entries collapse to the facts that still matter, dropping stale specifics

172	  cost of the benefit phasing in gradually rather than landing all at once.

174	  `_revise_candidates`'s bisection shape. Rejected: that batching exists
175	  because many candidates share one cached source-document prefix during
176	  `wakil enrich`; no equivalent shared prefix exists across unrelated

input.old_string:
## Decision

Two mechanisms, shipped together.

**1. `wakil entities compile [SLUG]`** — a new periodic/on-demand command
that re-synthesizes each entity's Compiled Truth from its full Timeline
history, favoring recency: recent entries keep concrete detail; older
entries collapse to the facts that still matter, dropping stale specifics
(a scheduled call that already happened, a "next steps" note superseded by
a later entry). Timeline itself is never touched by this operation —
it stays the complete, intact evidence log. Generalizes
`docs/entity-model.md`'s single-entity design into a workspace-wide sweep,
since "periodic" implies batch:

- No `SLUG`: workspace-wide due-scan (the periodic use case).
- `SLUG` given: compile that one entity now, ignoring the due-check (manual
  override, e.g. right after a big meeting).
- `--type`, `--min-timeline-chars`, `--dry-run`, `--yes`, `--commit` flags,
  mirroring `wakil schema migrate`'s existing plan/diff/confirm/apply shape
  (`schema_migrate_service.py`, `main.py:897-970`) — the closest existing
  precedent for a workspace-wide, non-source-scoped maintenance operation
  with a reviewable diff.

**2. Gated context-trimming**: once a note has been compiled at least once,
`wakil enrich`'s revision call sends only its Compiled Truth (not Timeline)
as context — directly attacking the size that caused the original
truncation. This is conditional, not universal: since most existing entity
notes have empty/placeholder Compiled Truth today, trimming unconditionally
would blind enrichment to most of what's actually known about most
entities until the whole vault has been compiled. The trim applies only to
notes carrying a fresh `compiled_through` marker (see below); everything
else keeps today's full-content behavior as a safe fallback. This couples
the two mechanisms by design: the context-cost benefit is earned per-note
by having run `entities compile` on it, not granted unconditionally. On a
freshly-migrated vault (nothing compiled yet), `wakil enrich` behaves
exactly as it does today — zero regression risk on day one — and cost
shrinks precisely as compilation coverage grows.

### Mechanism 1 (shared prerequisite): factor the note-section split out

`_merge_entity_note` already parses a note into "top section" (between H1
and the Timeline heading) and "Timeline section" via `_H1_RE` /
`_TIMELINE_HEADING_RE` (`ingest_service.py:1016-1085`). Factor this into a
reusable `_split_note_sections(content) -> tuple[Post, h1_line, top, timeline] | None`
helper, used by the merge path, the new compile path, and the gated
context-trim. Pure refactor — `_merge_entity_note`'s own behavior is
unchanged.

### Mechanism 2 detail: `entities compile`

- **New skill** `src/wakil/skills/entity-compile/SKILL.md`, distinct from
  `note-revision` — the judgment is genuinely different. `note-revision`
  merges *new* source material and treats "shorter than before" as a red
  flag; compile has no new source, re-derives Compiled Truth from the
  note's own full Timeline, and shortening old, superseded detail is the
  point, provided every still-true fact remains present somewhere (Compiled
  Truth or the untouched Timeline). Requires an `eval.json` live-model
  scenario before being considered production-ready, per this project's own
  norm for new judgment guidance (ADR 0004) — not just unit tests.
- **New contract** `EntityCompileOutput` (`src/wakil/llm/schemas.py`): one
  `compiled_truth: str` field. One entity per call, deliberately not
  batched like the revision call — there's no shared cacheable prefix
  across unrelated entities' Timelines the way there is across candidates
  sharing one enrich source document, so batching here buys nothing and
  reintroduces the exact truncation risk this ADR exists to reduce. Each
  call's size is bounded by that single note's own content, not compounded
  across entities. The residual risk of one pathologically long Timeline
  overflowing a single call is real (named in ADR 0015) and left as a
  surfaced warning, not solved by new chunking logic here.
- **New prompt builder** `build_compile_prompt(top_section, timeline_section)`
  in `llm/prompts.py` — simpler than `build_revision_prompt`, no source
  document or cacheable-prefix split needed.
- **New frontmatter field** `compiled_through: <date>`, stamped by
  `entities compile`, meaning "Compiled Truth already reflects every
  Timeline entry as of this date." Distinct from `updated:`, which is
  stamped on any content change including a plain Timeline append during
  `wakil enrich` and so can't distinguish "just grew" from "was actively
  re-synthesized." Due-check: never compiled and Timeline exceeds
  `--min-timeline-chars` (default TBD at implementation, e.g. 4000 —
  Timeline character length as a computable proxy for cost, the same
  precedent `_split_candidates_by_content_length` already established); or
  compiled before, but new entries past `compiled_through` push accumulated
  growth over that same threshold.
- **New service module** `src/wakil/app/entity_compile_service.py`
  (mirrors `schema_migrate_service.py`'s shape: `plan_entity_compilation`/
  `apply_entity_compilation`, own `CompileProposal`/`CompilePlan`
  dataclasses) rather than growing the already-1450-line
  `ingest_service.py` further. `apply_entity_compilation` re-reads each
  file immediately before writing and skips (reports, doesn't silently
  overwrite) anything changed since planning — the same stale-file guard
  `apply_migrations`/`apply_enrichment` already use. Reuses
  `_merge_entity_note`'s top-section-replace logic for the actual write,
  with `compiled_through` added to `frontmatter_updates` alongside
  `updated`; Timeline section passed through byte-identical.
- **New CLI group** `entities_app`, `app.add_typer(entities_app,
  name="entities")` — plural, matching the existing `sources` group
  precedent. `--commit` reuses the existing `"chore"` commit kind
  (`git_service.commit_change`), no `COMMIT_PREFIXES` change needed — same
  category as `schema migrate --commit`.

### Mechanism 2 detail: gated trim in the revision call

In `_run_entity_updates`, when building `candidates`, also read each
target's `compiled_through` frontmatter and Timeline size. A new
`_is_compile_fresh(post, timeline_section, min_timeline_chars) -> bool`
gate decides, per candidate, whether `build_revision_prompt` receives that
target's full content (today's behavior, the default) or just its top
section via `_split_note_sections` (once compiled and not yet stale).
`_merge_entity_note`'s merge step is unaffected either way — it always
re-reads the full file at apply time regardless of what the model saw,
since merging needs the real Timeline to prepend into.

### Passive nudge from `wakil enrich`

When `_run_entity_updates` touches a candidate whose Timeline has grown
past `min_timeline_chars` since its last `compiled_through` (or was never
compiled and already exceeds it), add one batched `proposal.warnings`
entry: "N entities have grown large enough to benefit from compilation —
run `wakil entities compile`." Visible, never auto-triggered — the same
advisory pattern already used for relevance exclusions and stale-file
skips, consistent with `CLAUDE.md`'s "avoid hidden background behavior."

## Decision

### Accepted: a single-entity, additive-only compile pilot

**`wakil entities compile SLUG`** (slug required, no workspace-wide sweep
yet) re-synthesizes one entity's Compiled Truth as the union of every fact
already present across its full Timeline history. **Additive only**: this
pilot does not implement "recent entries keep detail, older entries
collapse" lossy compression — the only validated problem (`docs/
entity-model.md`'s audit: Compiled Truth is empty/placeholder for most of
the vault) is fixed by synthesizing it at all, not by compressing it.
Additive synthesis has a safe failure mode by construction: worst case it's
verbose or redundant; it cannot silently drop a still-true fact the way a
"what's safe to compress" judgment can. Timeline itself is never touched —
it stays the complete, intact evidence log regardless.

- **No new skill file yet.** `note-revision/SKILL.md` already specifies
  exactly this judgment for the ordinary State-merge case: re-synthesize
  Compiled Truth as "the union of what was already there plus what's new."
  For compile, "what's new" is empty — the source *is* the note's own
  Timeline. Try driving the compile prompt off `note-revision`'s existing
  discipline before writing `entity-compile/SKILL.md` as a distinct
  judgment surface; only split it out if reuse proves genuinely awkward in
  practice (e.g. `note-revision`'s other Timeline-entry-specific guidance
  confuses the model when there's no new entry to append). This also means
  `EntityRevisionOutput`/`build_revision_prompt` may be reusable rather
  than needing a wholly new `EntityCompileOutput`/`build_compile_prompt` —
  confirm once real prompts are drafted, don't assume either way yet.
- **One call per entity**, no batching — the compile prompt has no shared
  cacheable prefix across unrelated entities' Timelines the way candidates
  sharing one `wakil enrich` source document do, so batching would add
  truncation risk without a caching benefit to offset it (unchanged from
  the original draft's reasoning here). The residual risk of one
  pathologically long Timeline overflowing its own compile call is real —
  notably, the notes most "due" for compilation (Mosaic ~53KB,
  edward-bridges ~32KB) are also the most likely to hit this — and is left
  as a surfaced warning, not solved by new chunking logic in this pilot.
- **`--yes`/`--commit` only, no `--dry-run` sweep flags yet** — those, and
  a due-check (`--min-timeline-chars`, `compiled_through` frontmatter
  field, workspace-wide scan), are explicitly deferred (see below), not
  part of what's accepted here.
- **Hard eval gate, not a soft IOU**: this pilot does not touch a real note
  outside of a live-model eval scenario (ADR 0004) run and reviewed first.
  ADR 0015's `relevance` field shipped with "required before considered
  complete" language and ran live before that eval existed — the resulting
  judgment instability (the same source's Brian Corr rated `central` in
  one run, `minor` in another) was only caught by accident, re-running the
  same source twice. Compile's failure mode is worse if wrong — Compiled
  Truth is what `wakil query`'s `_build_contexts` actually shows the user
  (the first ~2000 chars of the file, i.e. the H1 + Compiled Truth region
  for a compiled note) — so this pilot does not repeat that pattern.

### Rejected as specified: gated context-trimming in `wakil enrich`

An earlier draft of this ADR proposed a second mechanism: once a note
carries a `compiled_through` marker, `wakil enrich`'s revision call would
send only its Compiled Truth, not full content, cutting the context-cost
that (theoretically, for a single oversized note — see Context) risks
truncation. This is rejected as specified, not deferred-with-hope: its
safety argument — "`_merge_entity_note`'s merge step is unaffected either
way — it always re-reads the full file at apply time" — is factually wrong
about the code that now exists. `_run_entity_updates` reads each
candidate's content exactly once into `content`; that same in-memory
string flows through `_revise_candidates` (the model prompt),
`_apply_entity_revisions` (`old_content = by_path.get(...)`, the merge
input), and `apply_enrichment`'s stale-file guard (`update.old_content`,
compared against a fresh disk read) — there is no re-read at apply time.
Trimming that one shared string for the prompt would, for every compiled
candidate: silently mark up-to-date entities as "changed since prepared"
in the stale-guard (a trimmed string can never equal a fresh full read),
break `_merge_entity_note` (no `## Timeline / Log` heading left to find,
`_TIMELINE_HEADING_RE` fails to match, misreported as a shape violation),
and corrupt `_split_candidates_by_content_length`'s cost-balancing (it uses
`len(candidate[2])` as its proxy — exactly the field this mechanism would
selectively shrink). Fixing this requires carrying two separate content
values per candidate (trimmed-for-prompt, full-for-merge/stale-guard/
bisection-sizing) through `_EntityCandidate` and every function that
touches it — a real design change, not a refactor, and not something to
retrofit onto ADR 0015's just-landed, live-validated machinery without its
own dedicated design pass. Revisit as a separate, later ADR once the
compile pilot above has proven its judgment is trustworthy — there is no
value in shrinking `wakil enrich`'s context around a compile step whose
own output isn't yet trusted.

### Explicitly deferred, not part of this decision

- Lossy "collapse stale detail" compression (only additive synthesis is
  accepted now; revisit once additive compile is running and trusted).
- The workspace-wide due-scan / `--min-timeline-chars` / `compiled_through`
  frontmatter field / `--dry-run` sweep and the `entities_app` CLI group —
  all deferred until the single-entity pilot's judgment (and, if it turns
  out to be needed, a dedicated skill) is proven on real notes.
- Gated context-trimming in `wakil enrich` (rejected above, not deferred —
  but a redesigned version addressing the content-duality problem could be
  a legitimate future ADR).
- `--min-timeline-chars` as a truncation-risk predictor: if a due-check is
  built later, frame Timeline length as a *note-readability* proxy for
  humans, not a truncation-risk predictor — ADR 0015 already established
  that content length is a poor predictor of the (thinking-token-dominated)
  truncation cost this ADR's Context section discusses, for the same
  reasons that applied to its own batching decision.

32	~32KB) and landed two *reactive* mitigations: relevance-gating candidates

46	entity-model.md` (a design doc, not yet implemented) already proposes a

48	real vault finding "Compiled Truth is empty for most of the vault... well

53	concern, and it's what this ADR is actually justified by.
54

56	justification — not the full proactive complement to ADR 0015 an earlier
57	draft proposed. See Decision.

60	
61	### Accepted: a single-entity, additive-only compile pilot
62	
63	**`wakil entities compile SLUG`** (slug required, no workspace-wide sweep
64	yet) re-synthesizes one entity's Compiled Truth as the union of every fact
65	already present across its full Timeline history. **Additive only**: this
66	pilot does not implement "recent entries keep detail, older entries
67	collapse" lossy compression — the only validated problem (`docs/
68	entity-model.md`'s audit: Compiled Truth is empty/placeholder for most of
69	the vault) is fixed by synthesizing it at all, not by compressing it.
70	Additive synthesis has a safe failure mode by construction: worst case it's
71	verbose or redundant; it cannot silently drop a still-true fact the way a
72	"what's safe to compress" judgment can. Timeline itself is never touched —
73	it stays the complete, intact evidence log regardless.
74	
75	- **No new skill file yet.** `note-revision/SKILL.md` already specifies
76	  exactly this judgment for the ordinary State-merge case: re-synthesize
77	  Compiled Truth as "the union of what was already there plus what's new."
78	  For compile, "what's new" is empty — the source *is* the note's own
79	  Timeline. Try driving the compile prompt off `note-revision`'s existing
80	  discipline before writing `entity-compile/SKILL.md` as a distinct
81	  judgment surface; only split it out if reuse proves genuinely awkward in
82	  practice (e.g. `note-revision`'s other Timeline-entry-specific guidance
83	  confuses the model when there's no new entry to append). This also means
84	  `EntityRevisionOutput`/`build_revision_prompt` may be reusable rather
85	  than needing a wholly new `EntityCompileOutput`/`build_compile_prompt` —
86	  confirm once real prompts are drafted, don't assume either way yet.
87	- **One call per entity**, no batching — the compile prompt has no shared
88	  cacheable prefix across unrelated entities' Timelines the way candidates
89	  sharing one `wakil enrich` source document do, so batching would add
90	  truncation risk without a caching benefit to offset it (unchanged from
91	  the original draft's reasoning here). The residual risk of one
92	  pathologically long Timeline overflowing its own compile call is real —
93	  notably, the notes most "due" for compilation (Mosaic ~53KB,

67	Marking a block with `cache_control` only produces a cache hit if everything before it in the request — `system` included — is byte-identical to a previous call within the TTL. `build_system_prompt` (`skill_loader.py`) bakes each DAG stage's skill body + JSON schema into `system`, so the extraction/resolution/revision calls in one `wakil enrich` run never share a cache lineage even though they all send the same source document — their `system` differs first, breaking the prefix chain before it ever reaches the shared content. `cacheable_prefix` on `ModelClient.complete()` therefore only pays off *within* one call type (retries, and any future batched sub-calls of the same call), never *across* call types, unless `system` itself is made call-invariant — which has its own cost (skill/schema content would move into the user message, a weaker instruction-following position). Before assuming a shared block will cache across two different call sites, check whether their `system` is actually identical first.
68	
69	### `thinking.budget_tokens` doesn't exist on `claude-opus-4-8` and later — use `output_config.effort` or `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` instead
70	**Established:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** `docs/adr/0015-relevance-gated-entities-and-truncation-driven-batching.md` (Decision 2, Step A), `src/wakil/llm/client.py`'s `DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL`
71	
72	`AnthropicClient.complete` hardcodes `thinking={"type": "adaptive"}` with no way to bound how much of `max_tokens` thinking consumes before output starts. The obvious lever — `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` — returns a 400 error on `claude-opus-4-8` (this codebase's `DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL`) and every later model in the family (Opus 4.7+, Fable 5, Mythos 5), confirmed against Anthropic's live migration guide (platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/migration-guide.md) and not just assumed. The two levers that are actually available on this model, confirmed against the installed SDK's type stubs (`anthropic` package, `types/output_config_param.py`, `types/thinking_config_disabled_param.py`): `output_config={"effort": "low"|"medium"|"high"|"xhigh"|"max"}` (compatible with adaptive thinking, currently never set — the call runs at whatever server-side default applies), and `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` (eliminates thinking-token cost entirely, at the cost of whatever quality adaptive thinking buys). ### An entity-revision candidate's `content` is one shared in-memory value across prompt, merge, and stale-guard — trace all three before changing what it holds
**Established:** 2026-07-25 · **Source:** ADR 0016 review (rejected "gated context-trimming" design), `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`

`_run_entity_updates` reads each candidate's target-note content exactly once into a `content` string (part of the `_EntityCandidate` tuple), and that same in-memory value is reused three separate times downstream: as the model prompt's input (`_revise_candidates`), as the merge's `old_content` (`_apply_entity_revisions`, `by_path.get(...)`), and as the comparison baseline for `apply_enrichment`'s stale-file guard (`update.old_content`, checked against a fresh disk read at apply time). Nothing re-reads the file between prepare and apply. An ADR proposing to trim that string for just the prompt (to cut context cost) initially claimed the merge step was unaffected because it "always re-reads the full file at apply time" — checked against the actual code, it doesn't; the claim was simply wrong, and acting on it would have silently broken the stale-guard (a trimmed string can never match a fresh full read), the merge (no Timeline heading left for `_TIMELINE_HEADING_RE` to find), and `_split_candidates_by_content_length`'s cost-balancing (which sizes candidates by `len(content)`) all at once, for exactly the notes the change was meant to help. 1	---
2	name: note-revision
3	description: Merge new information into an existing note without losing what it already says — classify the change, re-synthesize State, append to Timeline, and preview before writing. Use whenever new facts about an already-noted person, company, project, or topic need to land on its existing page.
4	skill_api: 1
5	---
6	
7	# note-revision
8	
9	`content-synthesis` writes a new note from scratch. `note-conformance` checks
10	a note's shape once it's written. `note-revision` is the step in between,
11	for the case those two don't cover: a note **already exists**, and new
12	information — from `entity-enrichment`, `knowledge-research`, a fresh
13	source, or a user correction — needs to land on it without erasing what's
14	already there. Losing previously-captured knowledge while "updating" a page
15	is the single worst failure mode this skill exists to prevent.
16	
17	## When to use
18	
19	- New facts about a person, company, project, or topic arrive and a note
20	  for that subject already exists.
21	- Explicitly asked to update, revise, or merge new information into an
22	  existing note.
23	- An attached companion document (a prep note, an agenda) itself needs
24	  updating after the fact — e.g. checking off its own open questions in
25	  place once a meeting resolved them. `transcript` only writes that
26	  resolution into the *new* meeting note; updating the companion document
27	  itself is a merge into an existing note, which is this skill's job.
28	- **Not** for creating a note that doesn't exist yet — that's
29	  `content-synthesis`. Not for fixing frontmatter/slug/link shape with no
30	  new information to merge — that's `note-conformance`. If a revision also
31	  needs a fresh routing decision (the subject moved directories, a new
32	  entity was split out), hand that off to `note-routing`; don't decide it
33	  here. And don't assume a newly-mentioned entity (a spun-out company, a
34	  person who wasn't tracked before) clears the notability gate just because
35	  it's related to the note you're revising — that judgment belongs to
36	  `entity-resolution`; name it rather than deciding notability yourself.
37	
38	## Procedure
39	
40	- [ ] Step 1: **Read the existing note in full before writing anything.**
41	      Load its current State, Timeline, and frontmatter. You cannot
42	      classify a change as additive, contradicting, or duplicate against
43	      content you haven't read.
44	- [ ] Step 2: **Re-read the raw source for the new facts, not your memory
45	      of it.** See "Extraction integrity" below — never transcribe a
46	      figure, date, or quote from earlier in a conversation when the saved
47	      raw source is available to re-read at the moment of writing.
48	- [ ] Step 3: **Classify the new material** against what's already on the
49	      page: additive, contradicting/superseding, or a duplicate. See "The
50	      three-tier dedup heuristic" below.
51	- [ ] Step 4: **Apply the region-specific update discipline**:
52	      re-synthesize State, append to Timeline. Never regenerate the whole
53	      page from only the new source. See "State vs. Timeline" below.
54	- [ ] Step 5: **Diff your draft against the current page before saving.**
55	      If the new version is shorter, or drops a fact/frontmatter key that
56	      was there before, stop — you are very likely clobbering, not
57	      updating. See "The clobbering bug" below.
58	- [ ] Step 6: **Preview, don't auto-apply.** Surface the diff for
59	      confirmation before writing, the same as every other wakil write
60	      path. See "Preview before writing" below.
61	- [ ] Step 7: **Update provenance**, including the `updated:` frontmatter
62	      field, and hand off to `note-conformance` for a shape check before
63	      `kb-commit`.
64	
65	## State vs. Timeline: two disciplines, one page
66	
67	A knowledge page has two regions with opposite update disciplines. Get this
68	backwards and you clobber the page:
69	
70	- **State (Compiled Truth)** is *re-synthesized* on every update to cover
71	  the union of what was already there plus the new facts. "Rewrite the
72	  State section" means re-derive it from everything known, never replace it
73	  with only the newest source.
74	- **Timeline (Log)** is *append-only*. New dated entries are added; existing
75	  entries — including auto-generated back-link lines — are never deleted,
76	  rewritten, or reordered.
77	
78	Losing a previously synthesized fact is a regression, not an update.
79	
80	## The clobbering bug
81	
82	A cautionary case from a prior system, in outline: three related pages (a
83	company, a person, and a program) were each fully regenerated from a single
84	new transcript instead of merged into their existing content. "Rewrite the
85	State section" was misread as "replace the page with the newest source,"
86	and the regeneration silently deleted frontmatter, prior distilled history,
87	and Timeline entries that didn't happen to appear in that one transcript.
88	
89	The lesson: full-file regeneration is the *mechanism* that enables
90	clobbering. Prefer surgical edits — append a Timeline entry, edit the State
91	block — over rewriting an existing page wholesale. Treat "my new version is
92	shorter than the old one" as a stop-and-check signal, not something to wave
93	through.
94	
95	## The three-tier dedup heuristic
96	
97	Before merging a new fact into an existing note (especially a
98	tracker-style note that accumulates dated entries — updates, figures,
99	events), classify it against what's already recorded:
100	
101	1. **Exact match** (same subject, same date, same value) → it's a
102	   duplicate. Skip it; don't append a second entry for the same fact.
103	2. **Fuzzy match** (same subject, same date, a similar-but-not-identical
104	   value) → flag for review rather than silently picking one. This is
105	   often a correction or a rounding difference, not a new fact — don't
106	   guess which.
107	3. **Conflicting value** (same subject, same date, a materially different
108	   value) → add it with an explicit note that it conflicts with the
109	   existing entry. Never silently overwrite the earlier figure and never
110	   silently drop the new one.
111	
112	Only tier 1 is safe to resolve automatically. Tiers 2 and 3 are exactly the
113	kind of ambiguity that "Preview before writing" (below) exists to surface —
114	report the conflict, cite both entries, and let the confirmation step
115	decide.
116	
117	## Resolving conflicting sources
118	
119	When merging facts that come from more than one source, and they disagree,
120	apply source precedence rather than picking arbitrarily — highest authority
121	first: (1) the user's direct statements, (2) the note's existing
122	State (its current synthesized understanding), (3) Timeline entries (raw
123	evidence already on the page), (4) external sources (API enrichment, web
124	search). When two sources genuinely conflict, note the contradiction with
125	both citations in the Timeline — never silently resolve it by picking one.
126	
127	Attribute each claim to whoever actually said or clearly implied it, not
128	whoever it's about. When a founder describes their own company's numbers,
129	the holder of that claim is the founder, not the company — companies don't
130	speak, their employees do. A self-reported figure is written as
131	self-reported, not elevated to verified fact just because it's now the
132	newest entry on the page.
133	
134	## Extraction integrity
135	
136	Never trust working memory for a figure, amount, date, or quote you're
137	about to write onto a page. If the fact came from a saved raw source
138	(an ingested transcript, article, or captured email), re-read it from that
139	file at the moment of writing rather than recalling it from earlier in the
140	conversation — long-context recall degrades and transposes digits in ways
141	that silently corrupt exactly the kind of data this skill exists to merge
142	carefully.
143	
144	## Preview before writing
145	
146	Findings and proposed merges are informational until confirmed — this skill
147	never auto-applies a revision, the same way the rest of wakil's write path
148	never does. `ingest_service.py`'s enrichment DAG and
149	`schema_migrate_service.py`'s migration planner both split into a
150	plan/propose phase that touches nothing and a separate apply phase that
151	only runs after confirmation (`schema_migrate_service` even re-reads each
152	file immediately before writing and skips any file that changed since
153	planning, rather than overwriting it blind). Follow the same shape here:
154	produce the diff, show what's additive vs. what's flagged as a conflict,
155	and only write once that's confirmed.
156	
157	## Provenance and timestamps
158	
159	- Update the `updated:` frontmatter field (present on identity-type schemas
160	  such as `person`/`company`, alongside `created:`) when a revision lands —
161	  don't leave it stale after a real content change.
162	- Never invent or leave a placeholder date. If the new fact's date isn't
163	  known, say so explicitly rather than writing "recently" or today's date
164	  as a guess.
165	- Never replace a developed note with a freshly generated summary, even
166	  when the summary is accurate — a shorter, cleaner-looking page that drops
167	  prior detail is the clobbering bug wearing a different outfit.
168	
169	Once the merge is written and confirmed, hand off to `note-conformance` for
170	the shape/schema pass, then `kb-commit` to land it.
171

4	skill_api: 1
5	---
6	
7	# entity-compile
8	
9	`note-revision/SKILL.md` already defines the State/Timeline discipline this
10	skill runs on: Compiled Truth is *re-synthesized* on every update to cover
11	the union of what was already there plus what's new, and Timeline is
12	*append-only*, never touched by a synthesis step. This skill doesn't restate
13	that discipline — read it there. What's different here is narrower: there is
14	no new source. "What's new" is empty. The entire input is one entity's own
15	existing Timeline, and the job is to produce a Compiled Truth that actually
16	reflects it, for notes where synthesis never ran (docs/adr/0016's audit
17	finding: Compiled Truth empty or placeholder for most of the vault, with the
18	real content sitting unsynthesized in Timeline).
19	
20	## What this does
21	
22	Read the given Timeline in full. Write a Compiled Truth paragraph (or a few)
23	that is the union of every fact it contains — not a diff, not a rewrite from
24	memory of the entity, a synthesis grounded only in the Timeline text given.
25	
26	## Hard constraint: additive only
27	
28	This is not a compression or summarization task. Every fact already present
29	in the Timeline must be present, in some form, in the Compiled Truth you
30	write. Worst case, the result is verbose or a little redundant — that's a
31	safe failure. Dropping a still-true fact is not; it's the same clobbering
32	failure note-revision's three-tier dedup heuristic and clobbering-bug
33	warning both exist to prevent, applied here to a case where there's no new
34	source to classify a fact against — only the question of whether two
35	Timeline entries are the same fact restated or two distinct ones.
36	
37	**When in doubt, don't silently resolve it: include both.** If two entries
38	look like they might describe the same underlying fact (same subject,
39	close-but-not-identical dates or figures) but you're not certain, keep both
40	in the output rather than merging them into one or guessing which is stale.
41	A reader can tolerate two similar sentences; they can't recover a fact that
42	silently vanished.
43	
44	## What this does NOT do
45	
46	- **No lossy "collapse stale detail" compression.** Deciding what's safe to
47	  drop as outdated is a different, harder judgment with no calibration data
48	  behind it yet — explicitly out of scope for this skill version (ADR 0016).
49	  If an old Timeline entry is superseded by a newer one, say so in the
50	  synthesis (e.g. "originally X, later revised to Y") rather than silently
51	  omitting the earlier value.
52	- **Never proposes a Timeline entry.** Timeline is passed through to the
53	  caller untouched — not edited, reordered, or appended to. That's a
54	  property of how this skill is invoked (the caller never asks for a
55	  Timeline edit here), worth stating plainly anyway so a reader doesn't
56	  assume this is a general-purpose revision pass.
57	- **Not a substitute for note-revision.** A source with genuinely new
58	  information about an entity still goes through note-revision's ordinary
59	  merge; this skill only runs when the "new" material is nothing at all —
60	  just the entity's own accumulated history, unsynthesized.
61	
62	## Worked example
63	
64	`companies/mosaic-private-markets.md` is exactly the shape this skill exists
65	for: a large Timeline of dated interview and meeting notes, an empty or
66	placeholder Compiled Truth. Its Timeline might contain entries like:
67	
68	```text
69	### 2026-05-02 — intro call
70	- Mosaic is raising a $40M Series B, targeting a Q3 close.
71	- Lead investor not yet confirmed.
72	
73	### 2026-05-20 — follow-up with CFO
74	- Series B target confirmed at $40M; CFO says they're now in
75	  term-sheet discussions with two lead candidates.
76	- Use of proceeds: 60% platform engineering, 40% go-to-market.
77	
78	### 2026-06-14 — partner meeting
79	- One of the two lead candidates dropped out over valuation.
80	- Remaining lead (unnamed) has verbally agreed to term sheet;
81	  signing expected early Q3.
82	```
83	
84	These are related but not redundant: the raise size is confirmed across all
85	three, the lead-investor status changes entry to entry, and the
86	use-of-proceeds detail appears only once. A correct Compiled Truth keeps all
87	of it, distinctly:
88	
89	> Mosaic is raising a $40M Series B (target confirmed as of 2026-05-20),
90	> planned for a Q3 close, allocating proceeds roughly 60% to platform
91	> engineering and 40% go-to-market. Two lead-investor candidates were in
92	> term-sheet discussions as of 2026-05-20; one dropped out over valuation by
93	> 2026-06-14, leaving one remaining candidate who has verbally agreed to
94	> terms with signing expected early Q3.
95	
96	Note what this is *not*: it doesn't drop the use-of-proceeds split just
97	because it appeared in only one entry, and it doesn't silently pick "one
98	lead investor" as the final state without naming that the field narrowed
99	from two candidates to one over time — both entries' facts survive, in
100	synthesized form, even though the raw Timeline entries themselves are left
101	exactly as they were.

`git commit` and `git push`/`fetch` over SSH can fail with `sign_and_send_pubkey: signing failed for RSA "..." from agent: agent refused operation` / `1Password: failed to fill whole buffer` / `fatal: failed to write commit object`. This is 1Password's SSH agent integration (used for both commit signing and the `git@github.com:...` SSH remote) getting into a stuck/locked state, not a repo or credential problem.

**Why:** Observed twice in one session (2026-07-25/26, wakil project) — first as `git fetch`/`push` failures, later as `git commit` itself failing, both with the same underlying signature-agent error. Retrying the same command doesn't help; the user unlocking/restarting 1Password on their end resolved it immediately.

**How to apply:** If a `git commit`, `git push`, or `git fetch` fails with this class of error, don't retry blindly more than once and don't reach for `--no-gpg-sign`/disabling signing as a fix — flag it to the user as a 1Password SSH-agent issue needing their action (unlock the app, restart its agent helper), then retry once they confirm. Never bypass commit signing without the user explicitly saying so.

Explain this statement: 'The compile mechanism itself was narrowed from "lossy compression, workspace-wide sweep, new skill assumed" down to "additive-only, single-entity, reuse note-revision's discipline unless proven awkward"'

That sentence packs three separate before/after narrowing decisions into one line — let me unpack each.

**"Lossy compression" → "additive-only"**

The original ADR draft had the compile command actively deciding what to *drop*: "recent entries keep concrete detail; older entries collapse to the facts that still matter, dropping stale specifics." That's a real judgment call — deciding what's safe to discard — with zero calibration data behind it. Worse, we already had direct evidence in this same session that a much *simpler* judgment (ADR 0015's four-way `relevance` classification) was unstable run-to-run on identical input (the same entity rated `central` in one run, `minor` in another, on the same source). Compression is a harder judgment than that, and unlike `relevance` — which just decides whether to bother updating a page — a bad compression call writes directly into Compiled Truth, which is specifically what `wakil query` shows the user. So the accepted scope drops compression entirely: compile now only unions everything already in the Timeline into Compiled Truth. That has a safe failure mode by construction — worst case it's verbose or repeats itself, but it structurally cannot drop a fact that's still true, since it's not making any keep/discard decision at all.

**"Workspace-wide sweep" → "single-entity"**

The original draft's `wakil entities compile [SLUG]` treated no-SLUG as "compile everything due for it" — a periodic bulk operation with `--type`, `--min-timeline-chars`, `--dry-run` flags, mirroring `schema migrate`'s sweep shape. That's a lot of machinery (a due-check, a new frontmatter field to track it, CLI flags) built on top of a judgment nobody had actually seen run yet. The accepted scope requires a specific `SLUG` — no bulk mode, no due-check, no sweep flags. The reasoning: you don't want the first time you find out the compile judgment has a problem to be after it already ran across dozens of files unsupervised. Prove it works on a few real, deliberately-chosen worst cases (Mosaic's ~53KB note, Edward's own ~32KB note) before building the infrastructure to run it everywhere.

**"New skill assumed" → "reuse note-revision's discipline unless proven awkward"**

The original draft assumed from the start that compile needed its own `entity-compile/SKILL.md`, distinct from `note-revision`. But `note-revision/SKILL.md` already states the exact core principle compile needs — "Compiled Truth is re-synthesized on every update to cover the union of what was already there plus the new facts." For compile, "what's new" is just empty; the source *is* the note's own Timeline. Writing a whole new skill file without first checking whether the existing one already covers it is exactly the kind of speculative abstraction CLAUDE.md warns against, so the accepted decision was: try reusing `note-revision`'s discipline first, and only split out something distinct if reuse turns out to be genuinely awkward in practice.

That last one is worth a footnote, since it's the one place where the actual build didn't just take the cheap option: reuse *was* tried and judged genuinely awkward — most of `note-revision`'s procedure (re-read the new source, classify it as additive/contradicting/duplicate, the three-tier dedup heuristic, resolving conflicts across multiple sources) is built entirely around comparing *new* material to what's already on the page. Compile has no new material — everything's already there. So a short, distinct `entity-compile/SKILL.md` was written after all, but it explicitly cites and builds on `note-revision`'s State/Timeline principle rather than restating it, and that reasoning is now documented in the file itself (that was the one gap the workflow's verify phase caught — the first draft skipped straight to writing it without recording that reuse had actually been tried and rejected, not just assumed unnecessary).

The docstring is honest about it: *"only one page per slug is expected to exist in practice"* — that's a stated assumption, not a guarantee the code enforces.

**What actually happens with your `edward-bridges` example:** `directories` is a *sorted* set of every entity type's canonical directory — something like `["companies", "concepts", "people", "projects"]` alphabetically. The loop checks each in that order and returns the **first file that exists**, silently. So if both `companies/edward-bridges.md` and `people/edward-bridges.md` existed, `companies` sorts before `people` alphabetically — `wakil entities compile edward-bridges` would resolve to the company, not the person, with no error, no warning, nothing telling you a second match even existed. It would just quietly compile the wrong entity.

There's one partial safety net: the preview step (`print_entity_update_preview`) does show the full resolved path — `UPDATE companies/edward-bridges.md` — in the diff panel before you confirm. So it's not *invisible*, but it's easy to miss if you're not specifically checking the path rather than just skimming the diff content, and nothing actively flags "hey, this slug was ambiguous."

**Should the slug include the directory prefix?** I don't think it should be *required* — the whole point of a bare slug is the ergonomic win, and the overwhelming majority of the time there's exactly one match, so forcing everyone to type `people/edward-bridges` for the common case would be worse UX for no benefit. But the resolver should stop silently picking a winner when there's more than one match. The right fix is a hybrid:

- Bare slug still works when it's unambiguous (the common case, unchanged).
- If the slug matches files in *more than one* directory, raise a clear error listing every match and telling the user to disambiguate with a full path instead of guessing.
- Accept a full relative path (`companies/edward-bridges.md` or `companies/edward-bridges`) as an escape hatch for exactly that disambiguation case — which the resolver could support today almost for free, since it's just checking `is_file()` against a constructed path.

That's a small, well-contained fix to `_resolve_entity_slug` plus a couple of tests (one for the multi-match case, one confirming the existing single-match behavior is unchanged). ### Known issue: `_resolve_entity_slug` silently picks a winner on a cross-type slug collision
**Source:** PR #33 (`feat/entity-compile-pilot` branch), `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`, session discussion 2026-07-26

Good, important pushback — and I described this too reductively before. Let me correct the mental model, then be honest about what this actually does and doesn't solve.

**"Additive-only" doesn't mean "textually concatenate everything."** It means *informationally complete* — no still-true fact gets dropped — not "no synthesis happens." Deduplication, reorganizing by topic instead of by date, and showing a value's current state alongside how it got there are all explicitly in scope; what's forbidden is *deciding a fact no longer matters and leaving it out entirely*. Look at the actual worked example in `entity-compile/SKILL.md`:

Three Timeline entries, each restating or updating the same facts across different dates (a $40M raise mentioned three times, a lead-investor count that changes from two candidates to one), compile into:

> Mosaic is raising a $40M Series B (target confirmed as of 2026-05-20)... Two lead-investor candidates were in term-sheet discussions as of 2026-05-20; one dropped out over valuation by 2026-06-14, leaving one remaining candidate...

That's not three restated bullets glued together — the $40M figure is stated once, not three times, and the investor-count narrative is reorganized around *the fact itself* (how it evolved) rather than around *which meeting it was mentioned in*. That reorganization and deduplication is real, useful synthesis over raw Timeline, even with zero facts discarded. So it's not literally a "union" in the concatenation sense — that was imprecise wording on my part — it's closer to "deduplicated and reorganized, but never lossy."

This isn't just my reasoning about intended behavior, either — one of the three live eval scenarios (`redundant-entries-compile-without-duplication`) specifically tests exactly your concern: overlapping Timeline entries must compile into something non-repetitive, not just restated three times. It passed live against the real model before this shipped.

**But you're right that this doesn't fully answer "how is this helpful over the long run,"** and I should be straight about that rather than paper over it. What additive-only synthesis solves is the *currently broken* problem: most Compiled Truth sections are empty or placeholder today, so a reader has to dig through raw chronological Timeline to reconstruct current state at all. Deduped, reorganized-but-complete synthesis is a real improvement over that, even without any compression judgment. What it does **not** solve is the problem you're actually pointing at: over a long enough history, an entity's Timeline will accumulate genuinely stale detail (a since-superseded next-step, a logistics note that mattered for one day and never again), and additive-only synthesis is *structurally incapable* of trimming that — it can only ever grow. Eventually Compiled Truth would become a deduplicated-but-still-unboundedly-long paragraph, not the quick, current-state read it's supposed to be.

That's exactly the judgment the original ADR 0016 draft's "lossy compression" mechanism was for — deciding what's now safe to leave out. It wasn't eliminated from the design, it was explicitly staged: the adversarial review's position (which I agreed with) was that compression is a much harder, uncalibrated judgment, with a much worse failure mode than "verbose" if it's wrong, and it shouldn't be trusted until the safer additive mechanism has run for a while and proven the underlying compile judgment is sound at all. So the honest framing is: this pilot fixes "no synthesis is happening," not "synthesis never needs to shrink" — the second problem is real, deferred on purpose, not solved by what shipped.

# Incremental Summarization: Mechanism & Structure

## Core Algorithm

The procedure follows a **four-component loop**:

1. **Chunk Window**: New turns accumulate in a buffer (typically 10-20 turns or 15K-25K tokens) separate from the rolling summary
2. **Merge Prompt**: When threshold is reached, a model integrates recent turns into the existing summary
3. **Pruning**: The recent buffer is cleared (keeping last 2-3 turns for continuity)
4. **Continuity Injection**: Each new turn begins with the rolling summary injected into context

As the document states: "the model does 'update the existing summary with what just happened'" rather than performing one-shot compression of all history.

## Summary Structure & Distinction

The system treats the rolling summary as the **primary context artifact**, explicitly separate from raw history. The document emphasizes: "Store your rolling summary as a separate artifact outside the conversation history — a file, a database record, or a structured object in your agent's state."

The rolling summary uses **section-based organization** including: Objective, Decisions Made, Constraints, Work Completed, Current State, Open Questions, and Do Not Revisit categories.

## Retention Logic

The merge prompt specifies what to preserve versus update:

- "Preserve all decisions, constraints, and current work state from the existing summary"
- "Update sections that have progressed"
- "Overwrite superseded information (if a decision was reversed, show the final decision with a note it was revised)"

The system enforces a **target token budget** to prevent unbounded growth.

## Discussed Limitations

The document identifies potential failure modes:

- "Poor merge prompts produce summaries that silently drop decisions, duplicate information, or grow unbounded"
- Format drift over cycles can degrade quality: "If the format drifts, summary quality degrades"

However, it offers no explicit discussion of compounding errors or detail loss across many iterations—only mitigation strategies like full-rewrites every fifth cycle for longer sessions.

Summarize: what is the core technique or system architecture proposed, how does it decide what information to keep in a compressed/summarized form vs. what to discard or archive, does it maintain a separation between a full raw log and a compressed/current-state representation, what mechanisms prevent information loss or hallucination during compression, and what are the key evaluation findings about quality/accuracy of the compressed representation vs the full history. # Summary: Chain-of-Key Incremental Summarization

## Core Technique

The paper proposes **Chain-of-Key (CoK)**, a method using JSON-structured memory representations for incremental summarization. Rather than regenerating complete summaries from scratch, CoK dynamically updates existing structured representations with new information.

The architecture operates in three phases:
1. **Initial structured summary generation** from the first document using a predefined schema
2. **Chain-of-Key updates** via two operations: UPDATE (modifying existing keys) and ADD (incorporating new keys)
3. **Final summary generation** from the accumulated structured memory

## Information Retention Strategy

CoK employs a **hybrid approach** without explicitly maintaining separate raw logs:

> "dynamically identifies which new information needs to be added or updated within the existing structures"

The method uses programmatic JSON path generation to merge summaries incrementally. When token budgets are constrained, the system applies **lossy compression** using three criteria: redundancy elimination, frequency emphasis, and relevance filtering—prioritizing frequently-mentioned attributes as "likely the most important."

## Loss Prevention Mechanisms

1. **Structured format advantage**: JSON's hierarchical capabilities support "superior expansion and nesting capabilities" versus plain text, reducing information ambiguity

2. **Deliberate reasoning steps**: CoK breaks updates into substeps—identifying keys, matching existing keys, generating JSON paths—leveraging "the LLM's reasoning capabilities to tackle complex and multifaceted reasoning problems"

3. **Preservation constraints**: Instructions explicitly state: "Updates should never reduce the amount of information"

## Evaluation Findings

**Performance gains on two benchmarks:**
- SUMIE dataset: 40% F1 improvement (GUjson vs GUtext); additional 7% with CoK
- BookScore dataset: 14% improvement (GUjson vs GUtext); additional 4% with CoK

**Quality under compression:** With token limits (200-1000 tokens), CoK achieved 30% better F1 scores than text baselines while maintaining fewer total tokens, suggesting JSON encodes information more efficiently.

**Key tradeoff identified:** Structured representations retain more details but risk including trivial information, negatively affecting salience metrics in literary summaries.

Quote key passages verbatim.

# Anthropic's Context Engineering Guidance for Long-Running Agents

## Compaction/Summarization

**When and what to compress:**
Anthropic recommends compaction as "the first lever in context engineering to drive better long-term coherence." The approach involves taking a conversation nearing capacity limits, summarizing contents, and restarting with that summary.

**What to preserve:**
"The model preserves architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, and implementation details while discarding redundant tool outputs or messages."

**Structuring compressed summaries:**
Anthropic advises engineers to "start by maximizing recall to ensure your compaction prompt captures every relevant piece of information from the trace, then iterate to improve precision by eliminating superfluous content."

They highlight that "overly aggressive compaction can result in the loss of subtle but critical context whose importance only becomes apparent later."

One safe approach: "tool result clearing" – once a tool has been called deep in history, agents don't need raw results again.

## External Memory vs. In-Context Compression

Anthropic contrasts these approaches:

**Structured note-taking** provides "persistent memory with minimal overhead" through agents regularly writing notes external to the context window, then pulling them back later. Example: "Claude Code creating a to-do list, or your custom agent maintaining a NOTES.md file."

This enables agents to "track progress across complex tasks, maintaining critical context and dependencies that would otherwise be lost across dozens of tool calls."

Anthropic released "a memory tool in public beta on the Claude Developer Platform that makes it easier to store and consult information outside the context window through a file-based system."

## Sub-Agent Architectures

Rather than one agent maintaining state across entire projects, "specialized sub-agents can handle focused tasks with clean context windows" while "each subagent might explore extensively, using tens of thousands of tokens or more, but returns only a condensed, distilled summary of its work (often 1,000-2,000 tokens)."

This achieves "clear separation of concerns—the detailed search context remains isolated within sub-agents, while the lead agent focuses on synthesizing and analyzing the results."

## Deciding What's "Load-Bearing"

Anthropic provides **no explicit checklist** for identifying load-bearing information. Their general principle is: find "the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome."

They acknowledge the challenge: "The art of compaction lies in the selection of what to keep versus what to discard" and recommend empirical tuning rather than prescriptive rules.

## What each source actually does

**1. Medium — layered/cascade compression.** Cheapest reduction first, most expensive last resort: deterministic tool-output truncation → deterministic sliding window → LLM summarization only when both fail. Large content gets stored as an external artifact with a lightweight reference kept in context, not inlined.

**2. Incremental summarization — a bounded rolling summary, updated in place.** A structured summary (Objective, Decisions, Constraints, Current State, Open Questions...) lives as its own artifact, separate from raw history. Each merge pass explicitly preserves everything and only *overwrites* superseded values with a note ("originally X, later revised to Y") — this is close to identical to what our additive-only compile already does. The load-bearing difference: it **enforces a target token budget** to stop unbounded growth, and mitigates quality drift with a periodic full-rewrite ("every fifth cycle"), not just incremental patches forever.

**3. Chain-of-Key (arXiv) — the closest academic match.** Its core update rule is stated almost verbatim as our own constraint: *"Updates should never reduce the amount of information."* That's real, independent validation that additive-only incremental updates are a sound, published technique — not just a cautious first step we invented. But it's explicitly **not** the whole story: under a constrained token budget, it *does* apply lossy compression, using three concrete, semi-objective criteria — redundancy elimination (we already do this), **frequency emphasis** (facts repeated across multiple entries are treated as more important), and relevance filtering.

**4. Anthropic's own context-engineering guidance.** Compaction is size/capacity-triggered, not time-based. Their rollout methodology — *"start by maximizing recall... then iterate to improve precision by eliminating superfluous content"* — is exactly the staged sequencing we already committed to (additive-first, prove it, add compression later). They also describe external structured note-taking (a persistent file outside the context window) as their recommended pattern for long-running state — which is just... wakil's entire premise, Markdown notes as external memory. And notably: they give **no prescriptive checklist** for what's safe to discard, recommending empirical tuning instead — the same reason we deferred compression rather than guessing at rules.

## Compare/contrast to what we built

Two things are already well-aligned, not gaps:
- Our Timeline/Compiled-Truth split *is* the "full artifact + lightweight reference" pattern from source 1 and the "raw history + external structured summary" pattern from source 4.
- Our staged rollout (additive-only now, compression deferred until trusted) *is* Anthropic's own recommended sequencing, and Chain-of-Key's additive-update rule independently validates the mechanism itself, not just the caution around it.

One real, concrete gap, which is exactly what you flagged last turn: **we have no bounded target size and no defined trigger for ever introducing compression.** Every other source treats "what's the budget, and what happens when we hit it" as a first-class design question. Ours currently doesn't have an answer beyond "defer it" — which was the right call to *not build compression blind*, but it leaves the actual growth problem genuinely unaddressed, not just postponed with a plan.

## What's worth integrating

One thing I looked at and don't think is worth adopting: Chain-of-Key's structured JSON intermediate representation outperforms plain text under tight budgets, but converting Compiled Truth's internal representation to JSON cuts against this project's Markdown-as-source-of-truth bias (`CLAUDE.md`) for a benefit that mostly matters at token budgets much tighter than a single Markdown note's Compiled Truth section — flagging it rather than silently dropping it, but I wouldn't build it.

- **Stage 3 (only if still wanted):** the workspace-wide sweep ADR 0016 deferred, using the Stage 1 size trigger as its due-check instead of the vaguer `--min-timeline-chars` character-count guess.

8	# Periodic Entity Compilation and Gated Timeline-Context Trimming
9	
10	`status: accepted` covers a substantially narrower decision than this ADR's
11	original draft proposed. It went through adversarial review (see Sources)
12	that surfaced a verified, concrete defect in the original Mechanism 2
13	("gated context-trimming") design and a scope/risk case for shrinking
14	Mechanism 1 before building it. What's accepted: a single-entity, additive-
15	only compile pilot (Mechanism 1, narrowed). What's explicitly **rejected as
16	specified**, not deferred-with-hope: gated context-trimming in the
17	`wakil enrich` revision call (original Mechanism 2) and lossy "collapse
18	stale detail" compression. See Decision for exactly what that means and
19	why.
20	
21	## Context
22	
23	`wakil enrich`'s entity-revision call (`_run_entity_updates` /
24	`_revise_candidates`, `src/wakil/app/ingest_service.py`) inlines the
25	**entire current file content** of every candidate entity note into the
26	prompt (`build_revision_prompt`, `src/wakil/llm/prompts.py:175-226`). Entity
27	notes only grow — Timeline is append-only by design
28	(`note-revision/SKILL.md`) — so this cost is unbounded.
29	`docs/adr/0015-relevance-gated-entities-and-truncation-driven-batching.md`
30	diagnosed a real `ModelTruncatedError` from this (case study:
31	`companies/mosaic-private-markets.md` ~53KB, `people/edward-bridges.md`
32	~32KB) and landed two *reactive* mitigations: relevance-gating candidates
33	before the call, and bisecting a batch by content length after a truncation
34	occurs, capped at a bounded recursion depth. **As of this ADR's adversarial
35	review, that fix is implemented, tested, and live-validated against the
36	real originally-failing transcript** — the acute, observed truncation
37	failure is resolved. ADR 0015's own Consequences section still names one
38	narrower, currently theoretical gap neither of its mechanisms closes: "a
39	single entity whose own existing note is large enough to overflow the
40	budget by itself." That gap, not the (now-fixed) batch-truncation failure,
41	is the truncation-side motivation for this ADR — worth naming precisely,
42	since conflating it with the already-solved failure overstates how urgent
43	the truncation case for this ADR actually is.
44	
45	The independently real, and stronger, motivation is separate: `docs/
46	entity-model.md` (a design doc, not yet implemented) already proposes a
47	`wakil entity compile <slug>` command, motivated by its own audit of the
48	real vault finding "Compiled Truth is empty for most of the vault... well
49	over a hundred lines of raw, unsynthesized interview notes dumped into
50	Timeline instead" — the synthesis half of the note format's own two-part
51	design has never actually run for most entities. This is a knowledge-
52	quality problem, true regardless of whether truncation is also a live
53	concern, and it's what this ADR is actually justified by.
54	
55	This ADR proposes a narrow pilot toward that second, stronger
56	justification — not the full proactive complement to ADR 0015 an earlier
57	draft proposed. See Decision.
58	
59	## Decision
60	
61	### Accepted: a single-entity, additive-only compile pilot
62	
63	**`wakil entities compile SLUG`** (slug required, no workspace-wide sweep
64	yet) re-synthesizes one entity's Compiled Truth as the union of every fact
65	already present across its full Timeline history. **Additive only**: this
66	pilot does not implement "recent entries keep detail, older entries
67	collapse" lossy compression — the only validated problem (`docs/
68	entity-model.md`'s audit: Compiled Truth is empty/placeholder for most of
69	the vault) is fixed by synthesizing it at all, not by compressing it.
70	Additive synthesis has a safe failure mode by construction: worst case it's
71	verbose or redundant; it cannot silently drop a still-true fact the way a
72	"what's safe to compress" judgment can. Timeline itself is never touched —
73	it stays the complete, intact evidence log regardless.
74	
75	- **No new skill file yet.** `note-revision/SKILL.md` already specifies
76	  exactly this judgment for the ordinary State-merge case: re-synthesize
77	  Compiled Truth as "the union of what was already there plus what's new."
78	  For compile, "what's new" is empty — the source *is* the note's own
79	  Timeline. Try driving the compile prompt off `note-revision`'s existing
80	  discipline before writing `entity-compile/SKILL.md` as a distinct
81	  judgment surface; only split it out if reuse proves genuinely awkward in
82	  practice (e.g. `note-revision`'s other Timeline-entry-specific guidance
83	  confuses the model when there's no new entry to append). This also means
84	  `EntityRevisionOutput`/`build_revision_prompt` may be reusable rather
85	  than needing a wholly new `EntityCompileOutput`/`build_compile_prompt` —
86	  confirm once real prompts are drafted, don't assume either way yet.
87	- **One call per entity**, no batching — the compile prompt has no shared
88	  cacheable prefix across unrelated entities' Timelines the way candidates
89	  sharing one `wakil enrich` source document do, so batching would add
90	  truncation risk without a caching benefit to offset it (unchanged from
91	  the original draft's reasoning here). The residual risk of one
92	  pathologically long Timeline overflowing its own compile call is real —
93	  notably, the notes most "due" for compilation (Mosaic ~53KB,
94	  edward-bridges ~32KB) are also the most likely to hit this — and is left
95	  as a surfaced warning, not solved by new chunking logic in this pilot.
96	- **`--yes`/`--commit` only, no `--dry-run` sweep flags yet** — those, and
97	  a due-check (`--min-timeline-chars`, `compiled_through` frontmatter
98	  field, workspace-wide scan), are explicitly deferred (see below), not
99	  part of what's accepted here.
100	- **Hard eval gate, not a soft IOU**: this pilot does not touch a real note
101	  outside of a live-model eval scenario (ADR 0004) run and reviewed first.
102	  ADR 0015's `relevance` field shipped with "required before considered
103	  complete" language and ran live before that eval existed — the resulting
104	  judgment instability (the same source's Brian Corr rated `central` in
105	  one run, `minor` in another) was only caught by accident, re-running the
106	  same source twice. Compile's failure mode is worse if wrong — Compiled
107	  Truth is what `wakil query`'s `_build_contexts` actually shows the user
108	  (the first ~2000 chars of the file, i.e. the H1 + Compiled Truth region
109	  for a compiled note) — so this pilot does not repeat that pattern.
110	
111	### Rejected as specified: gated context-trimming in `wakil enrich`
112	
113	An earlier draft of this ADR proposed a second mechanism: once a note
114	carries a `compiled_through` marker, `wakil enrich`'s revision call would
115	send only its Compiled Truth, not full content, cutting the context-cost
116	that (theoretically, for a single oversized note — see Context) risks
117	truncation. This is rejected as specified, not deferred-with-hope: its
118	safety argument — "`_merge_entity_note`'s merge step is unaffected either
119	way — it always re-reads the full file at apply time" — is factually wrong
120	about the code that now exists. `_run_entity_updates` reads each
121	candidate's content exactly once into `content`; that same in-memory
122	string flows through `_revise_candidates` (the model prompt),
123	`_apply_entity_revisions` (`old_content = by_path.get(...)`, the merge
124	input), and `apply_enrichment`'s stale-file guard (`update.old_content`,
125	compared against a fresh disk read) — there is no re-read at apply time.
126	Trimming that one shared string for the prompt would, for every compiled
127	candidate: silently mark up-to-date entities as "changed since prepared"
128	in the stale-guard (a trimmed string can never equal a fresh full read),
129	break `_merge_entity_note` (no `## Timeline / Log` heading left to find,
130	`_TIMELINE_HEADING_RE` fails to match, misreported as a shape violation),
131	and corrupt `_split_candidates_by_content_length`'s cost-balancing (it uses
132	`len(candidate[2])` as its proxy — exactly the field this mechanism would
133	selectively shrink). Fixing this requires carrying two separate content
134	values per candidate (trimmed-for-prompt, full-for-merge/stale-guard/
135	bisection-sizing) through `_EntityCandidate` and every function that
136	touches it — a real design change, not a refactor, and not something to
137	retrofit onto ADR 0015's just-landed, live-validated machinery without its
138	own dedicated design pass. Revisit as a separate, later ADR once the
139	compile pilot above has proven its judgment is trustworthy — there is no
140	value in shrinking `wakil enrich`'s context around a compile step whose
141	own output isn't yet trusted.
142	
143	### Explicitly deferred, not part of this decision
144	
145	- Lossy "collapse stale detail" compression (only additive synthesis is
146	  accepted now; revisit once additive compile is running and trusted).
147	- The workspace-wide due-scan / `--min-timeline-chars` / `compiled_through`
148	  frontmatter field / `--dry-run` sweep and the `entities_app` CLI group —
149	  all deferred until the single-entity pilot's judgment (and, if it turns
150	  out to be needed, a dedicated skill) is proven on real notes.
151	- Gated context-trimming in `wakil enrich` (rejected above, not deferred —
152	  but a redesigned version addressing the content-duality problem could be
153	  a legitimate future ADR).
154	- `--min-timeline-chars` as a truncation-risk predictor: if a due-check is
155	  built later, frame Timeline length as a *note-readability* proxy for
156	  humans, not a truncation-risk predictor — ADR 0015 already established
157	  that content length is a poor predictor of the (thinking-token-dominated)
158	  truncation cost this ADR's Context section discusses, for the same
159	  reasons that applied to its own batching decision.
160	
161	## Alternatives considered
162	
163	- **Lossy "collapse stale detail" compression from day one**, the original
164	  draft's framing. Rejected for this pilot: the only validated problem is
165	  that Compiled Truth is empty, which additive-only synthesis already
166	  fixes with a safe failure mode (verbose, never wrong). Deciding what's
167	  "stale" has zero calibration data behind it and is exactly the harder,
168	  unvalidated judgment a sibling field (ADR 0015's `relevance`) already
169	  showed can be unstable run-to-run on identical input. Worth adding back
170	  later, once additive compile is running and trusted, as its own decision
171	  with its own eval — not bundled into the first cut.
172	- **A new `entity-compile/SKILL.md` immediately**, the original draft's
173	  framing. Deferred, not rejected: `note-revision/SKILL.md` already
174	  specifies "re-synthesize as the union of what was already there plus
175	  what's new," which is structurally the same judgment compile needs (with
176	  "new" being empty). Try that before assuming a distinct skill file is
177	  warranted — writing one prematurely is exactly the kind of speculative
178	  abstraction `CLAUDE.md` argues against if the existing discipline turns
179	  out to cover it.
180	- **Trim Timeline from every candidate's context unconditionally,
181	  immediately** (gated context-trimming's would-be simpler alternative).
182	  Moot for this pilot — gated context-trimming itself is rejected as
183	  specified (see Decision), so there's no trim to make unconditional or
184	  gated in the first place. Recorded for whoever picks up a redesigned
185	  version later: an unconditional trim would still blind enrichment to

211	- No `wakil enrich` cost reduction from this pilot — that was gated
212	  context-trimming's benefit, and it's rejected as specified. This pilot's

215	- The compile pilot does not touch a real note until it has a live-model
216	  eval scenario reviewed (ADR 0004) — a hard prerequisite for this ADR,

219	  existed.

242	## Sources

245	  (the reactive mitigations this ADR complements; names the "single large
246	  entity" gap this ADR still doesn't close)
